Knowledge Centre

Medical questions and answers

Collected answers to the questions asked most often across La Rose specialties and Knowledge Centre content.

Frequently asked questions

Clinical & Therapeutic Nutrition

A full medical assessment using the InBody device to determine your fat, muscle and water percentages and your measurements; body-contouring measurements to track progress; a full consultation with a specialist-grade clinical and therapeutic nutrition physician who reviews your labs and medical history; and the setting of the plan that suits your case: whether that is a nutrition plan, sessions or injectable therapy.

If you have recent labs, bring them, it saves time. If you do not, the doctor will specify what is needed after the consultation. If the plan will include weight-loss injections, there is a baseline panel we ask for first: CBC; TSH, FT3 and FT4; urea and creatinine; AST and ALT; HbA1c and fasting blood sugar.

No. No single plan works for everyone. The plan is built after we understand your body composition, your medical history and the real shape of your day, and it is adjusted every week according to how you responded and to what you were actually able to keep to.

The scale gives you one number. A body-composition analysis tells you what that number is made of: how much is fat, how much is muscle, how much is water. This matters because losing muscle looks like success on the scale while in fact it slows your metabolism and makes the weight come back. We follow composition, not the number.

Weekly follow-up is what keeps the plan alive and adapting to your body. A gap of more than a week counts as a new consultation, because the situation will have changed and needs assessing again from the start.

Start with one household change: more regular meal times, accessible water, vegetables or fruit with meals, and a suitable protein source. Do not put every age on one diet; children, pregnancy and chronic illness have different needs, and a medical condition requires an individual plan.

It depends on your food, age, symptoms, pregnancy or breastfeeding, health conditions, medicines and sometimes tests. A supplement is not universal insurance, and excess amounts of some nutrients can harm, so review the need and dose instead of starting a random collection.

Yes. Choose a meal with a protein source and vegetables, ask for sauces and extras separately, and decide the portion before eating from a large container. Review your repeated orders; improving the usual choice matters more than finding a perfect meal every time.

No. The written line should lead to the meal: lentil soup from the freezer with bread and salad, or chicken with vegetables and rice. Balance is judged across the day or week, and amounts vary by person [2, 3].

No. Thaw in the refrigerator, in cold water inside a leak-proof package with regular water changes, or in the microwave followed by immediate cooking. The surface can warm enough for microbial growth while the centre remains frozen [6, 7, 8].

Continuous freezing at 0°F (-18°C) or below preserves safety for a long time, while freezer times usually describe quality. Guidance gives three to four months as a general quality window for leftovers, but food and wrapping matter. Label the date and check the specific chart [7, 8, 9].

Usually, although texture after thawing varies. Divide rice and pasta promptly into shallow containers, cool safely, and reheat thoroughly. Bread is often practical, while cream sauce or lettuce may change texture. Follow product instructions [6, 7, 8].

Seek help for bloody diarrhoea, diarrhoea beyond three days, repeated vomiting that prevents fluids, high fever, or dehydration. Fever with flu-like symptoms during pregnancy, or symptoms in a young child, older adult, or immunocompromised person, justify earlier contact [10, 11].

It depends on the meal and the rest of your day. Oil raises energy density in a small volume, but it does not replace protein, vitamins, or minerals. If the meal lacks protein, yogurt, cheese, milk powder, or a suitable plant protein may be more useful; if protein is already present and volume is the barrier, an appropriate fat may be easier. The decision should consider total intake and health conditions, particularly kidney or liver disease or diabetes [3, 9].

Usually not at the start. Keep the meal and addition consistent, then record whether you finished, whether symptoms appeared, and whether the rest of the day was affected. Detailed calculation can help when a dietitian needs to compare intake with specific requirements, but it is not necessary to test one habit. What matters is that the addition is nutritious, repeatable, and part of a balanced pattern rather than simply extra sugar [1, 2, 3].

A nourishing drink helps some people, but for others it fills the stomach and reduces solid food. Try a small amount between meals rather than before the anchor meal and watch tolerance. If fullness starts after only a few bites or lasts for hours, especially with nausea, vomiting, pain, or marked bloating, do not respond only by adding more drinks; persistent early satiety needs medical assessment [1, 2, 4].

No. They are concentrated, nutritious additions, but sesame, tree nuts, and peanuts are major allergens. Avoid any ingredient to which you have a known allergy, and read labels for its presence or possible cross-contact. If facial or tongue swelling, breathing difficulty, wheezing, severe dizziness, or fainting occurs after eating, follow your prescribed emergency plan and seek emergency help immediately [11].

Only after the first addition is comfortable, repeatable, and does not reduce the rest of your intake. A week gives early tolerance information, while weight and strength trends need longer observation. If the goal still fits and there are no symptoms, discuss keeping the first change or adding one more small step. If weight keeps falling or you seem to need a large rapid increase, do not accelerate alone; review the cause and requirements with a professional [2, 3, 5].

If intake has been very low or almost absent for several days, or you are severely underweight or have had substantial recent loss, do not make a sudden nutritional jump on your own. Some people are at risk of fluid and electrolyte disturbances during refeeding and need a clinically planned start and monitoring. NICE provides specific risk criteria and cautious introduction guidance, so contact a clinician or nutrition team before proceeding [3].

No. One day describes that day and may expose useful questions about timing, drinks, or forgotten eating occasions, but it does not measure your usual diet or the adequacy of every nutrient. Intake varies from day to day, so estimating usual patterns requires multiple non-consecutive records or structured recalls selected for the assessment goal. Use the photos to begin a conversation, not to deliver a verdict [2, 3, 4].

Not for a simple record, although an after-photo can clarify leftovers when a substantial amount remains or the portion changes. Image-assisted assessment research sometimes uses before-and-after images to improve intake estimation. If that would make the day burdensome, take the starting photo and add a short note such as “left half” or “had a second serving” [1].

Not for this exercise. A photo, time, and brief description can support a useful discussion without numbers. Even formal dietary assessment contains measurement error, and an image cannot reveal every ingredient or cooking method. If a clinician needs weighing, household measures, or more days, they can request it for a defined purpose. Do not begin intensive counting on your own if it increases anxiety or rigid control [1, 2, 4, 9].

Photograph the dish as served and note what is clear: its name, fried or grilled preparation, sauce on the side, accompanying drink, or whether it was shared. A package or menu can preserve the item name, but do not guess grams or hidden ingredients. Visually similar dishes can differ in recipe, fat, or sugar, which is an important limitation of image analysis [1, 2].

It can be used as a descriptive record, but it does not change your care plan or medicine dose and cannot prove that a food is safe for your condition. Photograph a label or product name when relevant, and record medicine timing or symptoms only if your clinician requests it. Needs vary with the condition, tests, and treatment, so individual changes belong with your treating clinician or dietitian [2, 7, 8].

Stop if recording increases fear or guilt, makes you delay eating, reduce portions for the camera, retake images compulsively, or compensate with fasting, vomiting, or punishing exercise. These signs justify early discussion with an appropriate professional; eating disorders need specialist assessment and treatment, not a more complete album. Seek urgent care for fainting, severe dehydration, or rapid physical deterioration [9, 10].

Choose something simple combining protein with fruit or a carbohydrate, such as fruit and nuts when suitable, or crackers with a sealed nut-butter portion. Yoghurt or a cheese sandwich can work but should stay refrigerated until use. Variety matters more than a special breastfeeding product [1, 2, 6].

Do not leave a perishable sandwich out for hours. Take it from the refrigerator at feed time and refrigerate it within two hours, or one hour above 90°F (32°C). If you do not know how long it sat out, discard it rather than tasting it for safety [6, 7].

No. Nearby water prevents delay, but one feed does not equal one bottle. Drink to thirst and notice urine colour and frequency, dry mouth, and dizziness. Heat, vomiting, or diarrhoea changes needs, while a medically prescribed fluid limit takes priority over general advice [9].

Not in that simple way. Adequate food and fluid supports your health, but supply is assessed through the feed and the baby's signs, including swallowing, nappies, and growth trend. Pain, poor attachment, or too few nappies calls for early feeding and paediatric assessment [11].

Not everyone needs the same supplement. Iodine and choline needs rise, while vitamin D and other nutrients depend on diet and health, but unsupervised excess can cause harm or interact with medicines. Review the product and dose with a clinician or dietitian [1, 4, 5].

Seek immediate care for fainting, persistent dizziness, breathing difficulty, chest pain or a racing heart, severe headache or vision change, fever, heavy bleeding, one-sided leg pain or swelling, or thoughts of harm. Say that you gave birth within the past year; a snack cannot treat these signs [12].

No. Fish, eggs, pulses such as lentils and beans, soy foods, nuts, and seeds can all contribute protein, depending on the meal and your needs. Not every option freezes equally well: cooked egg within a dish or lentil soup may be practical, while other foods change texture. Vary your choices instead of relying on one food, and complete the portion with vegetables and a suitable starchy food [1, 2, 3].

A hand measure can be a rough household reminder, but it is not a prescription and does not represent every person's requirement. Needs vary with age, body size, activity, pregnancy or breastfeeding, illness, and goals, while actual protein differs between chicken, lentils, and yoghurt. If you need a number or have a medical condition, ask a professional to assess the whole day and then translate that range into repeatable portions [1, 4, 5, 12].

U.S. guidance gives three to four refrigerator days for most cooked leftovers and three to four freezer months as a general quality period for leftovers, although food type, wrapping, and temperature matter. Continuous storage at 0°F (-18°C) or below preserves safety longer, but quality may decline. Label the date and check the storage chart for the specific food [7, 8, 9].

No. Thaw it in the refrigerator, in cold water inside a leak-proof package with regular water changes, or in the microwave followed immediately by cooking or reheating. The surface can become warm enough for microbes to grow while the centre remains frozen. Some leftovers can be reheated from frozen, but they take longer and must heat thoroughly throughout [6, 7, 8].

Breathing difficulty, tongue or throat swelling, marked dizziness, or loss of consciousness after eating may signal a severe allergy and require immediate emergency action according to the allergy plan and local emergency services. Seek medical assessment for bloody diarrhoea, diarrhoea beyond three days, vomiting that prevents fluids, high fever, or dehydration such as little urination and dizziness on standing. Pregnant people, young children, older adults, and immunocompromised people need earlier contact [10, 11].

Possibly, but it is not proof by itself. The scale combines fat, muscle, water and digestive contents, while waist measurement is affected by tape position, breathing and bloating. A repeated direction using the same method, alongside suitable strength and energy or improving health indicators, is useful information. Confirming what the change means requires reading circumference with the weight trend and context, not turning one difference into a diagnosis. [1, 2, 4]

There is no single frequency suitable for everyone. Daily weighing may help one person view an average calmly and may increase anxiety for another. Waist measurement usually does not need daily repetition because small differences may come from technique or bloating. Agree a schedule that serves a clear decision, using the same scale, tape location and comparable conditions. If measuring sharply changes eating or mood, reduce its frequency and discuss an alternative with the professional. [4, 6]

Yes, it is possible, particularly if resistance exercise helps preserve fat-free mass while fat decreases; new exercise can also shift fluid temporarily. But stable scale weight should not automatically be labelled muscle gain. Examine the trend, measurement method, strength and performance, and if body-composition analysis is used, compare on the same device under similar conditions. [2, 7, 8]

Not necessarily. Bioelectrical impedance devices estimate components from the signal, body water and equations, so a short interval may capture fluid noise more than real tissue change. Frequency depends on the goal, device, expected size of change and whether the result would alter a decision. More important are the same device, a repeatable protocol, and interpreting the result with circumference, strength and symptoms rather than seeking a better report every week. [1, 2]

Do not automatically eat less because of one reading. First review the trend across several weeks, measurement quality, hunger, energy, protein, sleep, movement, medicines and symptoms. Aggressive restriction can harm nutrition and performance and make muscle preservation harder. If weight and measurements are truly stable, the professional can review the plan and goal and decide whether adjusting food or movement is appropriate instead of copying another person's energy deficit. [7, 11]

Arrange assessment for unintentional weight loss, reduced appetite, increasing weakness, unusual fatigue or new difficulty with ordinary tasks. Rapid gain with swelling needs faster review. Severe breathlessness, chest pain or heaviness, coughing blood, fainting or confusion requires immediate emergency care through local services. Do not wait for a new measurement, because a scale and body-composition test cannot diagnose the cause. [9, 10]

More hunger can be understandable because milk production uses energy, especially with exclusive feeding, broken sleep and delayed meals. Whether it is normal depends on severity and accompanying symptoms. New, intense hunger with marked thirst and urination, palpitations, tremor, unintentional weight loss or disabling fatigue deserves clinical review rather than being attributed to breastfeeding alone [1, 2, 10].

Severe restriction is not recommended because it makes energy and nutrient needs harder to meet and may worsen fatigue. The effect of any plan on feeding should be judged from the baby's signs, growth and feeding frequency, not from sensation alone. Use gradual changes, and if supply or growth is a concern, have a professional observe a whole feed and review your intake [2, 6, 7].

There is no magic menu or single food. The foundation is a varied pattern containing fruit and vegetables, carbohydrates, protein and suitable fat sources, with selected nutrients reviewed according to your health and eating pattern. A fully vegan diet or broad food exclusion calls for closer attention to vitamin B12, iron, iodine and other nutrients with professional guidance [1, 3, 8].

Drink to thirst and keep water available, but forcing very large amounts is not a substitute for frequent feeds and effective attachment. If supply is a concern, review feeding frequency, swallowing, nappies and growth with a professional. Vomiting, diarrhoea or very hot weather can increase fluid needs and may require appropriate replacement [4, 6, 7].

No, it is not automatically forbidden. Caffeine passes into milk in small amounts, and low-to-moderate intake usually does not cause a problem. Consider the total from coffee, tea, cola, energy drinks and chocolate, and reduce it if the baby becomes irritable or sleeps poorly, especially when premature or very young [1].

The decision is not identical for everyone. It depends on diet, previous anaemia or deficiency, health conditions, medicines and the product's contents. Review the label with a clinician or dietitian and do not combine several products that repeat the same nutrients. Iodine and vitamin D are important examples, but the parent's dose and the baby's supplement plan are separate decisions [1, 8, 9].

No, not by itself. It is one criterion used to screen adults for possible malnutrition, but a clinician interprets it with weight history, intake, strength, symptoms and examination. A person stable for years differs from somebody losing rapidly, and BMI does not describe body composition or the cause [3, 4].

There is no single suitable rate for everybody. The NHS describes roughly 300 to 500 extra calories daily as one possible adult starting point, but needs and response differ. Follow the trend over weeks and adjust with a professional rather than chasing a rapid change that may be fat, fluid or digestive distress [1, 3].

Not necessarily. They may help between meals when chewing, portion size or early fullness limits intake, but work best within a varied plan. Oral supplements have a role when needs are not met, and selection changes with diabetes, kidney disease, allergy and swallowing problems [1, 3].

The place of purchase or the word “herbal” is not a guarantee. Products differ and may cause sedation, other effects or medicine interactions. Even a studied medicine does not suit every cause or person. Review your full medicine list with a clinician or pharmacist and do not start or stop prescribed treatment alone [11, 12].

No plan can guarantee that every part of the gain will be muscle. Adequate energy, suitable protein and progressive resistance exercise support muscle building, but age, training, sleep and health influence the result. Follow strength, performance and body composition when indicated rather than expecting every kilogram to be muscle [8, 9].

Seek urgent care for dehydration or fainting, inability to keep fluids down, bloody vomit, black stool, severe pain, confusion or rapid deterioration. Persistent unintentional loss, swallowing difficulty, prolonged diarrhoea, palpitations, or increased thirst and urination need prompt assessment even when they are not emergencies [2, 5, 6, 7].

No. After weight loss, energy needs partly fall and appetite may rise while satiety falls, but this is adaptation of varying degree, not permanent “damage”. Review the trend, food, movement, sleep, medicines and symptoms with a clinician instead of ordering random tests or using a harsher diet. [4, 5, 7]

Not simply because PCOS is present. No single dietary composition has proved best for everyone. Carbohydrate amount, type and distribution should fit your needs, symptoms and results; the priority is a balanced pattern that can be repeated without harmful restriction. [2, 4]

No. Insulin resistance is important for many people with PCOS, but available assays have limitations and are not a stand-alone explanation for regain. The clinician selects glucose and risk assessment from history and symptoms and reviews sleep, medicines, eating and movement too. [2, 3]

A one- or two-day reading is often affected by water, salt, carbohydrate and bowel contents and cannot identify a change in body fat. Return to the usual routine without compensatory starvation and follow a several-week trend under similar measurement conditions. [4, 5]

No medicine guarantees a permanent result for everyone. A medicine may fit a defined goal after assessment, but benefit, harm, duration and pregnancy plans must be reviewed with the prescriber. Do not start, stop or restart it independently. [1, 2, 7]

Prompt review is appropriate for rapid or unexplained gain, especially with swelling, weakness, palpitations or a marked cycle change. Sudden swelling with breathlessness, chest pain or fainting requires immediate emergency care; do not assume it is body fat or wait for another weigh-in. [1, 2, 11]

Not necessarily. Fasting glucose, HbA1c and the oral glucose tolerance test do not always identify the same people, so one can be in range while another shows abnormal glucose regulation. That does not mean everyone needs all three; a clinician selects or repeats testing according to risk and the clinical question [2, 3, 5].

No. The pattern may be consistent with greater compensatory insulin secretion, but it must be read with the unit, laboratory interval, fasting duration, simultaneous glucose, medicines and health context. Differences between insulin assays mean there is no single worldwide value that proves the diagnosis for everyone [1, 6].

No. These symptoms can follow a large or unbalanced meal, insufficient sleep, anaemia, medicine or other causes, while insulin resistance and prediabetes may cause no symptoms at all. Record the timing, meal and accompanying features, and let a clinician decide whether glucose testing or another assessment is appropriate [1, 10].

Not automatically for everyone. HbA1c can add a view of recent months, but it has limitations with anaemia, altered red-cell lifespan, pregnancy and other circumstances. A clinician selects it when it helps the question and investigates disagreement with glucose rather than relying on one number [2, 4].

No. Complete elimination or prolonged fasting is not required and may be unsuitable for your health or medicines. A sustainable balanced pattern with fibre, protein, vegetables, a suitable amount of carbohydrate, activity and sleep is more useful. Individual details belong with a professional, especially during pregnancy or with chronic illness [1, 8, 12].

Timing depends on age, risk factors, symptoms and previous results; there is no single schedule for everyone. Guidance allows different follow-up intervals, and a clinician may repeat sooner or use another test when suspicion is high. Intense thirst and urination or unintended weight loss calls for faster medical contact rather than waiting for routine retesting [1, 5, 7, 10].

Usually fasting. Fasting insulin and HOMA-IR are calculated from a fasting glucose and insulin sample, and eating beforehand raises both, so the reading stops being meaningful [6, 7]. Fasting plasma glucose itself is taken after at least 8 hours without food, usually in the morning [3], while HbA1c ordinarily needs no fast [4]. The exact fasting time and medicine timing are set by the clinician and laboratory, so do not stop any medicine yourself. There is also no single "normal" HOMA-IR value that fits everyone, so the result is read against the laboratory reference and your own situation [7, 8].

No. The pattern may be consistent with the pancreas compensating by releasing more insulin, but it is not standalone proof. The unit, laboratory interval, fasting duration, glucose from the same sample, medicines and risk factors all need review. Differences between insulin assays also prevent one universal number from applying across laboratories [6, 8].

There is no single worldwide cut-off suitable for every age, population and laboratory. HOMA-IR is derived from fasting glucose and insulin; research thresholds vary with the population and assay, and clinical use is limited by the lack of uniform reference values. Do not treat an online calculator result as a diagnosis without clinical review [6, 7, 8].

No. Fasting plasma glucose requires a fast according to laboratory instructions, and an oral glucose tolerance test has specific preparation and steps, whereas HbA1c ordinarily does not require fasting. Do not guess from the test name; follow the clinician's and laboratory's instructions, and do not stop medicine by yourself before sampling [2, 3, 4].

No. These symptoms can follow a large or unbalanced meal, insufficient sleep, anaemia, medicines or other causes, while insulin resistance and prediabetes often cause no clear symptoms. Record the timing, meal and accompanying features, and let a clinician decide whether glucose testing or another assessment is appropriate [1, 12].

Not always. Without unequivocal hyperglycaemic symptoms or a glucose crisis, diagnosis usually requires confirmation with another result at an appropriate time. Classic symptoms with clearly raised glucose can change both the diagnostic route and urgency. Do not delay medical contact when intense thirst and urination, vomiting or rapid deterioration are present [2, 3, 13].

Do not select the test by yourself. PCOS is linked with a higher risk of impaired glucose tolerance and diabetes. Endocrine guidance recommends an oral glucose tolerance test for glycaemic screening in PCOS, with HbA1c considered when the tolerance test cannot be completed. The treating clinician should decide the test and timing according to pregnancy, symptoms and earlier results [11].

Not necessarily. You can be stressed and physically hungry at the same time, and eating may simply coincide with your usual meal. Stress-related eating has no gold-standard diagnostic test, and stress affects people differently. Consider the context: your last meal, hunger, trigger, any sense of lost control and recurrence. One episode does not diagnose a disorder [2, 3, 8].

No single rule says complete removal is right for everyone. Severe deprivation can increase cravings and guilt for some people. It is often more useful to reduce automatic eating: choose an amount, sit down, notice the food and keep satisfying alternatives available. If a particular food is repeatedly linked to loss-of-control episodes, discuss it within specialist care instead of creating harsh rules alone [1, 4, 7].

Punishment and restriction can increase hunger and restart the cycle, particularly when episodes recur. Return to your usual pattern at the next eating opportunity instead of compensatory fasting, unless your clinician has provided different advice for a medical or personally relevant religious context. Vomiting, laxatives and harsh exercise are not safe compensation methods and need clinical discussion if they occur [7, 11].

It depends on the pattern. A trained nutrition professional reviews meal regularity, hunger and medical nutrition needs, while a mental-health professional assesses anxiety, depression, trauma or loss of control and provides appropriate psychological treatment. When recurrent binges, compensatory behaviour or marked distress is present, collaboration is often better than choosing one discipline and ignoring the rest. The initial assessment can guide referral [7, 8, 13].

Yes. Weight does not have to change for eating behaviour to cause distress or affect mental health and daily life. Eating-disorder guidance warns against using BMI or illness duration alone to decide who deserves treatment. Loss of control, secrecy, shame, compensatory behaviour, or effects on work and relationships are sufficient reasons to request assessment [7, 9, 10].

If the pattern recurs or escalates, becomes your only soothing strategy, feels uncontrollable, or accompanies persistent anxiety or depression, request assessment instead of adding restrictions. Seek urgent help for physical deterioration, dangerous compensatory behaviour or thoughts of self-harm. Impact and safety matter more than waiting for an arbitrary number of days [7, 8, 13].

Not in the simplistic way often described. The body digests and absorbs amino acids, but uses them across many tissues and functions; not every extra amount goes to muscle building. The muscle response to a meal has practical limits shaped by body size, age, exercise and meal type, so distributing suitable sources through the day is usually more useful than believing in one fixed magic number. [3, 5]

Not automatically. Powder is convenient and measured, but it does not always provide the variety, fibre and other nutrients found in food. It may help when there is a genuine gap or low appetite, while food is enough for many people. The choice depends on need, tolerance, ingredients, illness and medicines, not product advertising. [3, 11]

Reviews of trials in healthy adults did not find deterioration in change in filtration with higher intake during the study periods, but this is not permission for any amount or a lifetime guarantee. If you have kidney disease, urine albumin or an abnormal result, the question is entirely different and your target needs to be set with the treating team. [8, 9]

Plant sources differ in amino-acid proportions, amount and digestibility, but a varied pattern with adequate energy can meet the needs of most healthy adults. Use pulses, grains, soy, nuts and seeds across the day without forcing a prescribed combination into every dish. Special situations need individual planning. [1, 12]

Not before reviewing the whole picture. Stable weight is not failure when strength or measurements improve, and limited muscle gain may relate to the training programme, energy, sleep, time or illness. If intake is below your needs, raising it to an appropriate level may help; if it is already adequate, another increase is not guaranteed to add benefit. [4, 5]

Seek emergency help immediately for sudden tongue or throat swelling, difficulty breathing or swallowing, severe wheeze, confusion or fainting; these may indicate a life-threatening allergy. Persistent vomiting or diarrhoea, palpitations, severe pain or dehydration after a new product also needs prompt assessment, and you should take the container with you. [11, 13]

No, drinking plain water, black coffee, and unsweetened tea without milk, creamers, or sugar does not break your metabolic fast, as these calorie-free fluids do not stimulate insulin secretion or elevate blood glucose [1, 3, 12]. Maintaining generous hydration throughout the fasting window is clinically vital to prevent dehydration, headaches, and constipation commonly experienced during the adaptation phase [3, 12]. However, adding even small amounts of sugar, milk, creamer, or caloric sweeteners triggers digestive responses and halts the fasting state [1, 3].

Light to moderate physical activity, such as walking, can safely be performed during the fasting window, but strenuous resistance training and heavy lifting are best scheduled during or shortly before the eating window [1, 3, 5]. Muscle protein synthesis and cellular repair require the timely availability of circulating amino acids, carbohydrates, and fluids post-workout [3, 5]. Training intensely near the end of an extended fast can induce acute dizziness or fatigue and may increase muscle catabolism rather than promoting hypertrophy [1, 5].

A weight loss plateau typically occurs because intermittent fasting does not automatically guarantee a caloric deficit if meals consumed within the eating window are calorie-dense and exceed daily expenditure [2, 3, 5]. Prolonged daytime restriction often triggers intense rebound hunger, leading individuals to inadvertently overconsume refined carbohydrates and fats during evening hours [3, 5]. Robust clinical trials confirm that time-restricted eating only produces sustained fat loss when total daily energy intake remains below expenditure, irrespective of the fasting duration [2, 7].

While intermittent fasting can improve insulin sensitivity under strict clinical supervision, it poses grave risks for individuals taking insulin or sulfonylurea medications that lower blood glucose [3, 6, 9]. American Diabetes Association guidelines emphasize that prolonged fasting without proactive medication titration can provoke hypoglycemia that may become dangerous [6, 9]. Therefore, you must never initiate fasting independently; your treating physician must adjust pharmacological doses and establish a frequent glucose monitoring plan first [6, 9].

The timing of your eating window significantly impacts metabolic outcomes due to endogenous circadian rhythms [8, 12]. Some small feeding studies suggest that eating earlier in the day (e.g., between 8:00 AM and 4:00 PM) may improve insulin sensitivity and glucose control in some people compared with eating late [8, 12]. Conversely, delaying food intake into late evening hours moves meals closer to melatonin release and sleep, which may fit less well with the body clock [8, 12].

Telogen effluvium (temporary hair shedding) and micronutrient deficiencies can develop if intermittent fasting involves severe, unstructured caloric reduction or poor food diversity [3, 4, 14]. Compressing daily intake into narrow windows often leads individuals to consume inadequate protein, dietary iron, zinc, and fat-soluble vitamins [3, 14]. Furthermore, rigid dietary rules can heighten psychological stress and trigger disordered eating behaviors in vulnerable individuals, necessitating immediate discontinuation and specialist dietary support [4, 14].

White pasta and refined pizza dough consist of rapidly digested carbohydrates that cause a sharp rise in blood glucose. The pancreas secretes a substantial surge of insulin, which subsequently drops blood sugar rapidly and triggers hunger cues in the brain. Lacking sufficient protein, fibre, and healthy fats, the meal clears the stomach swiftly without eliciting long-lasting satiety hormones [9, 10, 13].

Drinking a glass of water before or with a meal can help if mild dehydration is present or if thirst is being confused with hunger. However, water cannot substitute for food and will not sustain satiety if the meal lacks sufficient protein, fibre, or total energy to meet your body's physiological requirements [1, 10].

Physical hunger emerges gradually, is experienced in the stomach as rumbling or emptiness, and is satisfied by any wholesome food. Emotional or stress-induced eating develops abruptly with intense urgency, fixates on specific sweet or salty comfort foods, and rarely yields feelings of true satiety even after eating [12, 14].

It may very likely represent reactive hypoglycemia, which occurs when the pancreas overproduces insulin after a high-glycemic meal. This drops circulating blood sugar, generating shakiness, cold sweating, dizziness, and palpitations alongside hunger, and warrants clinical assessment to rule out insulin resistance [4, 7, 13].

When persistent hunger is accompanied by excessive thirst, frequent urination, and unintended weight loss, it may indicate diabetes mellitus. When hunger occurs alongside weight loss despite abundant intake, heat intolerance, hand tremors, and resting palpitations, it suggests an overactive thyroid [1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8].

A physician selects targeted diagnostic tests based on your clinical history and symptoms, typically including fasting glucose, HbA1c, fasting insulin, thyroid function tests (TSH, free T4), and a complete blood count, alongside a thorough review of regular medications [1, 2, 3, 13].

No. One episode or one occasion of overeating is not enough for diagnosis. A professional assesses loss of control, recurrence over time, distress, accompanying features and effects on your life. Seek help before any time threshold is reached if the episode concerns you, recurs or involves compensation [1, 3, 6].

Formal diagnosis considers the amount relative to the time and circumstances together with loss of control, but difficulty estimating quantity does not erase your distress. Tell the clinician what happened and how it felt instead of trying to prove a number. Recurrent loss of control deserves discussion even when you are unsure of the amount [1, 10, 12].

Do not punish yourself with restriction or compensatory fasting. Return to adequate, regular eating opportunities because harsh restriction and hunger can maintain the cycle. If a condition or medicine requires specific meal timing, follow the treating clinician's plan and do not alter it yourself [3, 5].

Yes. Eating disorders can occur across body weights and shapes, and weight alone does not measure loss of control, distress or risk. Do not wait for weight gain; speak with a professional when episodes recur or affect you [2, 6].

Not everyone needs medicine, and it is not something to start yourself. Eating-disorder-focused psychological care and regular eating are important foundations. Selected medicines may be discussed after diagnosis and review of risks, interactions, and physical and mental health [3, 7, 10].

Start with a simple direct sentence: “I have episodes of rapid eating when I feel unable to stop, and I need help arranging an assessment.” Choose someone you trust and make a specific request, such as listening without judgement or accompanying you. Support does not replace professional care, but it can make the first step easier [2, 4].

Yes. This is not a contradiction. A difficult event may occur long after your last meal, leaving you in need of both energy and comfort. Eat a suitable meal or snack when hunger is present, and add an emotional response such as a short rest or contact with someone you trust. Do not use the presence of emotion to deny a bodily need [1, 3, 4].

No. Rumbling or emptiness is one possible clue, but many people notice hunger as reduced concentration or energy, irritability or increasing interest in food. Routine, illness and medicines can also alter cues. Consider timing, the adequacy of the last meal and the whole group of signals, and consult a clinician when a change is new, severe or persistent [1, 2, 11].

Not definitely. A sudden urge for a specific taste can be linked to a situation or emotion, but intense hunger, smell, habit and food availability can do the same. Ask about the last meal, context and sensations, and observe several episodes rather than judging one desire [1, 2, 3].

Do not turn observation automatically into prohibition or punishment. Eating for pleasure or comfort sometimes is not a disorder. Pause, check for hunger and choose consciously. Add another soothing response when possible so food does not become your only tool. If the pattern is recurrent or out of control, seek support rather than imposing harsher rules [1, 2, 9].

It can help when it stays brief and neutral: timing, hunger, situation, feeling and what followed. Calories and weighing are unnecessary. If recording increases obsession, guilt or restriction, stop and discuss an alternative with a professional. Monitoring is a tool for understanding a pattern, not a test or punishment [1, 2, 10].

Seek specialist assessment when loss of control, secretive eating, marked distress or compensatory behaviour recurs, or the pattern affects daily life. Fainting, dehydration, chest pain, vomiting blood or risk of self-harm requires urgent help. Do not wait for weight to change before speaking up [5, 6, 7, 10].

No. One occasion is not enough for a diagnosis. A clinician considers recurrence, loss of control, distress, compensatory behaviour and the effect on your health and life. Emotional eating can occur without a disorder, but deserves support when it becomes recurrent or your only way to self-soothe [1, 4, 6].

No. Eating disorders and distressing eating patterns can occur across body weights and shapes, and weight alone does not measure distress or risk. Speak with a professional if there is loss of control, secretive eating, compensation or disruption to daily life, even when weight is stable [5, 6, 9].

It depends on the pattern, and the two often complement each other. Nutrition care supports adequate regular eating and reduces restriction; a mental-health professional is essential with recurrent loss of control, anxiety, depression, trauma or compensation. A doctor joins when physical symptoms or medical monitoring are present [6, 9, 10].

Usually, harsher rules are not the answer. Restriction can increase hunger and preoccupation with food and feed the eating-and-guilt cycle. Binge-eating treatment focuses on regular eating, understanding triggers and building emotional coping skills, rather than making weight loss the primary treatment goal [6, 8, 11].

It can help when it stays simple and non-judgmental: note timing, hunger, situation, feeling and what followed. This can reveal a pattern to the clinician. If recording becomes compulsive counting or increases guilt and restriction, stop and discuss an alternative; monitoring is a treatment tool, not punishment [6, 8].

Fainting or confusion, chest pain or severe palpitations, vomiting blood, dehydration or inability to keep fluids down, profound weakness, and repeated self-induced vomiting or laxative misuse need urgent assessment. Thoughts of self-harm or suicide, or any immediate danger, require local emergency help now [5, 6, 10].

No. It is a supporting clue, especially when weight has been stable since childhood, but it does not cancel new loss or symptoms. Constitutional thinness is considered after excluding disease, eating disorders, inadequate intake and excessive exercise while reviewing the full weight history [1].

Not necessarily. It is an underweight category and a screening measure, not a diagnosis by itself. It should be interpreted with weight trajectory, intake, strength, symptoms and the proportion of any unintentional loss [2, 4].

There is no fixed list. History and examination direct a blood count, iron, glucose, thyroid or coeliac testing—or other tests—when indicated. A random package can miss the context and produce incidental results unrelated to the problem [4, 6, 7, 8].

Stability is more reassuring than new loss, but assessment is useful when intake is poor, weakness or symptoms are present, BMI is very low, or there is concern about an eating disorder or nutrient deficiency. The whole picture determines the decision [1, 4, 9].

Not on your own. The starting point is usually structured eating opportunities, appropriate energy and protein fortification, suitable movement and monitoring. Medicines and supplements have indications, contraindications and interactions, so a clinician decides whether one has a role for you [4, 10, 11].

You do not need a fixed grain-and-pulse combination in the same dish at every meal. The body uses amino acids supplied by different foods across the day. A varied pattern containing pulses, grains, nuts or seeds and soy—with eggs or dairy if chosen—can meet the needs of most healthy adults when total food and energy are adequate. Focus on a recognisable protein source and daily variety rather than worrying about each mouthful [2, 4].

No. Spinach can contribute iron, but it cannot guarantee adequate status by itself, and absorption of plant iron varies with the meal and the body's needs. Use several sources such as lentils, fava beans, chickpeas, other beans, fortified cereals, nuts and seeds, and pair them with vitamin-C-rich food. When symptoms, blood loss or pregnancy are present, assessment and testing matter more than increasing one food [6, 7, 12].

Eggs and dairy contain B12 and can contribute, but adequacy depends on amount, regularity, age, medicines and the ability to absorb it. Someone who eats very little of these foods, has symptoms, uses metformin or long-term acid suppression, or has had gastrointestinal surgery needs individual review. The name of the dietary pattern alone cannot establish B12 status [2, 9, 10].

Do not start treatment-dose iron on your own: excess can be harmful, and it is important to establish whether deficiency exists and why. For B12, timing depends on symptom severity and the possibility of neurological involvement, pregnancy or malabsorption. When neurological disease or rapid deterioration is a concern, a clinician may start replacement without waiting for every result. Seek prompt advice rather than delaying or self-treating [6, 10, 12].

There is no single interval for everyone. Timing depends on the nutrient, severity, treatment, underlying cause, symptoms, pregnancy, chronic disease and possible malabsorption. A clinician may repeat a full blood count, iron markers or B12 at different times and may also track symptom response. Agree on a specific follow-up point before leaving the visit rather than repeating tests every few days on your own [8, 10].

Yes, but suitable means planned and monitored, not merely meat-free. Pregnancy and breastfeeding require review of energy, protein, iron, B12 and other nutrients, and a vegan pattern needs a reliable B12 source. An athlete must match energy, protein and meal distribution to training. The plan should be individualised with the treating clinician and dietitian rather than built around random doses or powders [1, 5, 13].

No. Carbohydrate remains part of pregnancy nutrition; the usual task is to adjust amount, type, timing, and distribution rather than eliminate it. Choose fibre-rich sources, eat whole fruit instead of juice, and review your readings with a dietitian. Severe restriction or a ketogenic diet is not a plan to begin independently during pregnancy [4, 5].

There is no single breakfast for everyone. Morning hormones, carbohydrate type and amount, dinner timing, sleep, and treatment can all affect the result. Start with the agreed meal, record the outcome, and change one element with the team. Do not independently remove breakfast, milk, or fruit because of one reading [2, 3, 5].

No. “Diet” does not make a product beneficial or unlimited, and some products contain carbohydrate from other ingredients. Water remains the simplest everyday drink. Read total carbohydrate and serving size, and ask the obstetric clinician or dietitian about any sweetener or product you use frequently during pregnancy [4, 5].

Record the result, test time, food, activity, and medicine, and check that handwashing and meter use were correct. Do not fast, delete the next meal, or take extra medicine independently. Follow your team’s instructions on repeat testing or contact, and report a repeated pattern; the food plan or treatment may need adjustment [2, 3, 4].

It does not mean failure. Insulin resistance rises with pregnancy changes, and food plus activity may not be enough even with careful adherence. Adding treatment aims for safer glucose for parent and fetus. Continue adequate nutrition and take medication at the dose and time prescribed by the team [1, 3, 4].

Glucose commonly improves after birth, but testing is still required at the time set by the team, with periodic follow-up afterwards. Pregnancy can occasionally uncover diabetes that was already present, and gestational diabetes raises the likelihood of later type 2 diabetes and recurrence in another pregnancy. Do not wait for symptoms before follow-up [1, 2, 9].

A diagnosis of insulin resistance does not mean you have diabetes or that you are inevitably destined to develop it; many individuals maintain compensatory hyperinsulinemia for years, keeping blood glucose within normal laboratory limits [1, 2, 4]. Rather, insulin resistance represents an early, highly modifiable metabolic warning sign. Timely lifestyle interventions—improving dietary composition, engaging in regular physical activity, and achieving modest visceral fat reduction—frequently restore insulin sensitivity and halt progression toward prediabetes or type 2 diabetes [1, 4, 10].

Complete or drastic elimination of all carbohydrates is neither medically mandatory nor generally sustainable in the long term, often triggering dietary fatigue and rapid weight regain [1, 5, 7]. Clinical guidelines prioritize carbohydrate quality, portion control, and meal composition over absolute bans: choosing unrefined, fiber-rich complex carbohydrates such as whole grains, oats, and legumes, and pairing them with adequate lean protein, healthy fats, and vegetables to flatten postprandial glucose excursions [5, 7, 11].

A single HOMA-IR reading should never be used in isolation to diagnose insulin resistance or dictate a clinical treatment plan. While HOMA-IR is a helpful mathematical model derived from fasting glucose and insulin values, commercial insulin assays lack universal international standardization, leading to variable reference ranges across different laboratories [2, 3, 4]. Comprehensive clinical assessment interprets this index in conjunction with waist circumference, blood pressure, lipid profiles, HbA1c, and family metabolic history [2, 4, 6].

An InBody test does not assess serum biochemistry or replace laboratory glucose and hormone assays, but it provides precise, objective data regarding internal tissue distribution [2, 7, 12]. It enables clinicians to quantify visceral fat levels around internal organs, skeletal muscle mass, and extracellular water balance, ensuring that body composition improvements and visceral fat reduction are clearly tracked even when the bathroom scale appears temporarily stagnant [2, 7, 12].

Yes, insulin resistance is profoundly linked with menstrual irregularities and subfertility in women, most prominently in those living with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) [8, 9]. Elevated circulating insulin acts directly on ovarian theca cells to stimulate excess androgen production while suppressing hepatic sex hormone-binding globulin, impairing follicular development and resulting in oligo- or anovulation; improving insulin sensitivity through dietary and lifestyle management frequently restores ovulatory cycles [8, 9].

Structured lifestyle intervention, nutritional optimization, and physical exercise remain the cornerstone and primary therapeutic approach for insulin resistance; pharmacological therapy is never an automatic default or a substitute for healthy habits [1, 2, 5]. However, an evaluating clinician may consider adjunctive medications like metformin in select clinical circumstances—such as documented prediabetes with high-risk features like severe adiposity, a history of gestational diabetes, or in managing symptomatic PCOS—after evaluating renal function and individual tolerability [1, 2, 5].

No. Some devices display an estimate related to abdominal fat, but it is not a direct image of fat around the organs. The equation, device and body shape all affect that estimate, so read it alongside waist size and risk factors rather than turning it into a diagnosis by itself. [3, 5, 6]

Usually not. Check the device, timing, food, drink, exercise and any fluid change, then ask whether the direction repeated and whether strength, waist or laboratory results support it. A major change based on one reading may be a reaction to measurement variation unless the clinician identifies a clear clinical reason. [3, 4, 8]

Body weight combines water, fat, fat-free tissues and digestive contents. One component can rise while another falls, and a device may interpret a water shift as a change in fat-free mass. Repeated measurements under consistent conditions, together with strength, waist and health context, are needed to judge whether the difference is meaningful. [3, 4, 8]

There is no universal schedule. Frequency depends on the goal, the measurement method, the time needed for a real change to emerge and whether the result would change the plan. Daily scanning often magnifies noise and anxiety, so agree on a meaningful review point with the treating clinician or nutrition professional. [3, 4, 7]

Yes, especially with BIA devices that estimate composition from electrical conduction and body water. Food, fluids, exercise and fluid distribution across the day can shift a reading, although the size of the effect differs by device and person. Follow the centre’s instructions and repeat under similar conditions rather than trying to correct the number yourself. [3, 4, 8]

Seek earlier assessment for continuing unintentional weight loss, new or worsening swelling, marked weakness, fainting, breathlessness, severe pain, dehydration or persistent appetite loss. These symptoms need assessment of their cause and should not wait for the next scan. If symptoms are severe or sudden, use the local urgent-care pathway. [10, 12]

No. The device measures electrical properties such as impedance, then its equations estimate body water, fat, fat-free mass and muscle. The result is a useful monitoring estimate, not a direct image of tissue or an independent diagnosis. [1, 7, 8]

It is a composite number produced by the device software from selected estimates, not an independent medical standard or a universal target. Ask what influenced it and whether its movement genuinely relates to your goal and health. [3, 8]

Estimated muscle is linked to body water and fat-free mass, so fluid intake, meals, exercise, illness or timing can move the number before true tissue change occurs. Compare one device under similar conditions across several visits. [5, 7, 9]

A direct comparison is often misleading because electrodes, frequencies and equations differ, and agreement with reference methods varies between devices. Treat each device as a separate trend and keep one device where possible. [8, 10, 11]

No. The number alone cannot diagnose disease. A clinician reviews it with waist, history, blood pressure, symptoms and selected tests where needed. Accuracy also varies with device, body size and fluid state. [2, 3, 9]

No. Assessment considers strength and performance with muscle quantity or quality, and may include grip or chair-rise testing and examination. The field can raise a question but is insufficient for diagnosis. [4, 6]

Not necessarily. Fat may fall while fat-free mass is preserved, or fluid shifts may temporarily hide the direction. Review measurements, strength, energy, symptoms and testing conditions across more than one point before judging. If the agreed goal is not progressing, the clinician should review the plan rather than infer the cause from the scale alone. [1, 2, 5]

It provides more estimates than body weight alone, but more information does not mean a final truth. The result depends on the device, equation, fluid balance and procedure. Its main value is following a trend on the same device under similar conditions and interpreting it alongside other indicators. [1, 2]

Devices may use different frequencies, electrodes, equations and reference populations, while your measurement conditions may also differ. Do not merge the two series as if they were the same method. Record the device and conditions, and use one device for the main trend where possible. [2, 3]

It can help some people notice a trend, and one study associated it with better results within a structured programme. It is not required and is unsuitable if it increases anxiety, restriction or impulsive decisions. Choose the frequency with a clinician according to the goal and the number's effect on you, not a universal rule. [4, 6]

No. Estimated muscle mass is one piece of information. European consensus starts with muscle strength and adds muscle quantity or quality and performance for diagnosis. If there is new difficulty rising from a chair, walking or carrying usual items, seek clinical assessment rather than relying on the report alone. [9]

Unintentional loss or continuing weakness and poor appetite need medical review. Sudden or severe swelling needs faster assessment, and swelling with breathlessness, chest pain or fainting requires immediate emergency care. These symptoms have their own assessment pathways; a fat-and-muscle report does not exclude a medical cause. [10, 11]

No. PCOS occurs across body sizes, and weight is not one of its diagnostic requirements. A person at their usual weight may still need follow-up of cycles, glucose, lipids and symptoms. Goals follow the health picture and personal preference, not an assumption that everyone must lose weight. [1, 2, 5]

Not to the same degree, and it cannot be diagnosed from body shape or sugar cravings. Insulin resistance is an important factor for many people with PCOS, but a single insulin measurement has limited value in routine care. The clinician selects glucose and risk assessment according to history, age and results. [2, 4, 8]

No. Multiple follicles can appear on ultrasound without the syndrome, while some cases are diagnosed from ovulatory dysfunction and androgen excess without requiring ultrasound. A clinician combines criteria and excludes similar causes, with different rules for adolescents. [2, 3, 4]

There is no evidence that one diet composition is best for every person with PCOS, and PCOS alone is not a reason to remove gluten. The amount, type and distribution of carbohydrate are tailored to needs, symptoms and results; any medical elimination needs its own indication. A balanced pattern that can be repeated without harmful restriction matters more. [2, 9]

Weight management may improve some features for people at a higher weight, but response is not guaranteed and loss is not everyone's goal. Irregular periods may need specific treatment and protection of the womb lining, so do not wait for weight loss when periods have been absent for a long interval. Decide with the clinician according to goals and pregnancy plans. [2, 3, 4]

PCOS can disrupt ovulation and make conception harder, but it does not mean pregnancy is impossible. Assessment covers ovulation and fertility factors in both partners, with treatment directed by a gynaecologist or fertility clinician. Do not start an ovulation medicine or supplement yourself, especially when pregnancy is possible or other medicines are used. [2, 6, 7]

Not necessarily. Many people can meet their needs through ordinary food distributed across meals. A supplement may be a practical tool when intake is inadequate or appetite is low, but it is not automatically better than food. Review ingredients, dose, kidney and liver health, and medicines with a clinician before use. [4, 5]

Walking is very useful for cardiovascular health, movement and consistency, but it may not give every muscle enough resistance to preserve strength. Guidelines add strengthening activity for the major muscle groups on at least two days each week. The starting level and exercise type should fit your health, joints and ability. [6, 7, 8]

Yes. It can be genuine progress when fat or measurements improve while strength and fat-free mass are maintained. Fluid can also hide a short-term trend. Follow several indicators over a suitable period instead of judging from one day or comparing two different devices. [6, 11, 12]

There is no single number for everyone. Evidence supports adequate or enhanced intake to help preserve muscle, but the target changes with body size, age, activity, total intake, and kidney and liver health. Ask a clinician to set a practical target for your situation rather than copying a number online. [4, 5]

No single outcome occurs to the same degree in everyone. Studies report changes in fat-free mass during weight loss, but this is not all skeletal muscle, and measurement, age, health, food and activity matter. Follow strength, intake and symptoms with the prescriber rather than relying on a general percentage. [10, 11]

Worsening weakness, falls, or new difficulty walking or rising from a chair needs review. Sudden weakness, especially on one side, or weakness with speech difficulty, fainting, chest pain or severe breathlessness requires immediate emergency care. Do not assume every episode of weakness is simply low protein without assessment. [1, 8, 9]

No. Vitamin B12 is an exception; plant foods do not naturally contain it unless fortified, regardless of how varied vegetables, pulses and grains are. [1]

It can be safe when well planned, according to the position of specialist medical bodies, but it needs a reliable vitamin B12 source from the start, because deficiency in the infant can affect neurological development in a way that is only partially reversible if diagnosis is delayed. [2, 3]

Not always. Bariatric surgery, long-term metformin, chronic gastritis or bowel conditions, and older age are all separate risk factors for B12 deficiency regardless of diet type, and can also combine in the same person. [4, 5]

Repeated vomiting, clear lethargy, failure to gain weight, low muscle tone, or loss of a previously gained skill such as sitting or babbling, especially if the mother follows a fully vegan diet or one without a documented B12 source. These signs call for a prompt visit, not waiting for the routine follow-up appointment. [3]

No. Do not rely on them unless that specific product is fortified with vitamin B12 and states the amount on its label. Some foods contain vitamin-like analogues but are not a reliable substitute for fortified food or an appropriate supplement [6, 8].

Not necessarily. Neurological, balance or sensory symptoms can occur without obvious anaemia, so the absence of anaemia or enlarged red cells does not rule out deficiency when symptoms and risk factors are present [7].

There is no single fasting duration for every device and every clinical situation. Food and fluid can matter, although studies report different effect sizes. Follow the provider's instructions and keep the interval from the last meal similar at each follow-up. Do not use severe fasting or delay prescribed medicine or fluid without asking the doctor. [1, 5, 6]

Keep a normal, safe drinking routine and follow the provider's instructions. The aim is similar conditions, not avoiding water all day or drinking a large amount at once. Dehydration and rehydration can appear as changes in fat or muscle, so tell the team if intake was clearly unusual. [4, 5]

Hard exercise and sweating can alter fluid, skin temperature and impedance, making comparison less fair. One clinical statement advises avoiding sweat-producing exercise for eight hours before measurement. If exercise occurred, do not automatically discard the result; record its type and timing and let the clinician decide whether to repeat it. [1, 8]

A direct comparison may mislead because devices differ in frequencies, electrodes, equations and calibration. If the device changes, retain both reports but treat the new one as the baseline of a new series, then follow the trend within that device alongside other indicators. [1, 2, 3]

Not as a universal requirement. A contact-electrode study found no significant composition differences between cycle phases, although some people notice swelling or weight changes. If you have a clear pattern, record it and keep timing similar where practical without treating the cycle as a proven explanation for every difference. [10]

First review the device, timing, food, fluid, exercise, illness and medicines. If the difference would change a decision, the clinician may repeat the test under conditions closer to baseline; there is no fixed interval for everyone. Unintentional loss, sudden swelling or breathlessness require medical assessment rather than waiting for another measurement. [1, 11, 12]

Not necessarily. A person can have a normal weight and still have muscle weakness that needs separate assessment; weight alone is not a sufficient indicator. [1, 2]

New difficulty climbing stairs or rising from a chair, unusual fatigue, or a noticeable slowing in walking are all signs worth mentioning to a clinician, even if weight is stable or falling. [2]

Usually above the usual reference amount, but the exact number is set with a nutrition clinician based on your situation, not a generic figure for everyone. [3]

Not necessarily to the same degree for everyone; the proportion varies considerably between individuals, which is exactly why functional screening matters with any appetite-reducing medicine, rather than assuming one outcome for all. [4]

No. A device estimates body components, while clinically meaningful muscle loss requires interpretation with strength, function and health context. Hydration, device method and test conditions can change the result [2, 7].

Usually not. Very frequent measurements may mostly reflect fluid shifts rather than real tissue change. Agree an interval that fits the goal and condition, use the same method under similar conditions, and follow strength and performance too [6, 7].

No. Some needs are identified from life stage or dietary history, while others, such as vitamin D and iron, require a targeted test. A clinician selects testing when the result will change the decision [1].

No. Even naturally occurring vitamins and minerals cause harm at high amounts: too much vitamin D can cause nausea and kidney stones, and too much iron can damage the liver and, at very high doses, become dangerous [4, 5].

Not always. Some supplements interact with each other or with medicines you take, and some products on the market have been found to contain different doses or ingredients than the label states. Show your full list to your clinician or dietitian before combining more than one product [2, 3].

No. A natural substance can have strong effects, toxicity or medicine interactions, and product quality varies. Safety depends on the ingredient, amount, health condition, medicines and manufacturing [2, 6].

Yes. Ingredients such as biotin can interfere with some laboratory methods and create misleading results. Tell the clinician and laboratory every product and amount before testing, and do not stop prescribed treatment on your own [7, 8].

No. More ingredients increase duplication and interaction risk and make side effects harder to trace. Prefer a product that matches a clear need in a known amount after reviewing diet, medicines and indicated tests [1, 3].

Not at all; medical nutrition therapy encompasses a broad spectrum of medical conditions far beyond weight loss [1, 2, 7, 10]. Clinicians design specialized nutritional protocols to manage prediabetes, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, and gout [2, 7, 10]. It also addresses functional gastrointestinal disorders, food intolerances, unintentional weight loss, malnutrition, and perioperative nutritional optimization [1, 2, 11]. The objective centres on metabolic health and systemic wellbeing rather than scale weight alone [1, 2, 10].

You do not need to order a new battery of lab tests specifically before your visit [2, 7, 10]. The most practical approach is bringing any blood tests or medical evaluations completed over the previous three to six months [2, 7, 10]. During your initial consultation, the physician conducts a physical examination and comprehensive history, ordering only targeted tests—such as HbA1c, fasting lipids, or renal and liver panels—indicated by your clinical presentation, preventing redundant expense [2, 7, 10].

An evidence-based clinical practice does not distribute standardized, pre-printed diet sheets to patients [2, 3, 10]. Your first consultation focuses on identifying metabolic requirements, work schedules, family routines, and food preferences [2, 3, 10]. The clinician collaborates with you to construct an individualized nutritional plan with flexible portioning and nutrient-dense choices that support your health sustainably, refining recommendations over time [2, 3, 10].

A stable scale weight initially does not signify that your metabolism has stalled or that the plan has failed [1, 4, 5, 10]. Standard bathroom scales are heavily influenced by transient fluid shifts, intestinal contents, hormonal fluctuations, and muscle glycogen storage following new exercise routines [1, 4, 5]. The clinician tracks progress using waist measurements and longitudinal InBody scans, confirming actual fat reduction and muscle preservation rather than overreacting to single-day scale fluctuations [1, 4, 5, 10].

You must never stop or adjust prescribed dosages independently when altering your diet [2, 7, 8]. Dietary modifications—especially moderating refined carbohydrates and dietary sodium—can rapidly enhance insulin sensitivity and lower blood pressure, requiring coordinated, gradual dose reductions by your treating physician to avoid dangerous hypoglycemia or hypotension [2, 7, 8]. Close medical oversight ensures safety during dietary transitions [2, 8].

Follow-up appointments are generally scheduled every two to four weeks throughout the initial two to three months of care [2, 3, 10]. This interval provides sufficient time for physiological adaptation, allowing the clinician to evaluate body composition changes, address social or dietary challenges, and adapt meal structures progressively as your metabolic health improves [2, 3, 10]. Once stability is established, appointments transition to monthly or periodic maintenance reviews [2, 10].

Frequently asked questions

Weight Management & Non-surgical Alternatives

The options we use are medically approved and widely used. But the real safety comes from how they are used: a dose titrated gently, baseline labs before starting, and weekly follow-up. Some cases are ruled out after the consultation and the labs, pregnancy and breastfeeding among them. Your safety matters to us more than anything.

Yes, there is more than one medically approved option, and they differ in how they work and in their effect on appetite and on insulin resistance. Choosing between them is not a general rule and not something to settle online: it is decided at the consultation from your case, your labs, your history and how you respond to the first doses.

For many cases, yes, and that is exactly why a lot of people come to us after being frightened by the idea of an operation. But not every case. At the consultation we assess the degree of obesity, your health status and your history, and if your case genuinely needs surgery we will say so and refer you to the bariatric surgery department.

It comes back if nothing else has changed. That is why we never give the injections on their own: they always run alongside a nutrition plan and weekly follow-up, and then a maintenance plan. The injections help you through the hard stage; what holds the result is the habits built along the way.

Most people get through this part smoothly. You may notice some changes in digestion in the first days of each new dose, such as feeling full earlier, and they usually settle on their own. That is exactly why the dose is stepped up gently rather than jumped, and why the weekly follow-up is there: we hear how you are doing and adjust the plan around you.

Yes, and it is not a formality. The labs show the thyroid, sugar, liver and kidney picture, and they often reveal the reason the weight was stuck in the first place. If you have recent results, bring them and we will review those rather than repeat them.

The rate differs from person to person with the starting point, the labs and how the plan is followed, and any guaranteed number quoted before a consultation is not an honest one. What we aim for is loss that is steady and comes from fat rather than muscle, and that is what the weekly follow-up measures.

Exercise is not a condition for the weight to come down, but it is what protects muscle and makes the final result look better. We start from what your life actually allows, even if that is a short walk, and build gradually. A plan you cannot follow is not a plan.

No. This is a prescription treatment with follow-up, and the consultation is what decides whether it suits you at all, which option and which dose. That step is not paperwork: it is what makes the treatment safe.

There is no single schedule for every medicine or person. An increase depends on the active ingredient, current dose, time on it, response and side effects. Do not raise the dose or shorten the interval yourself; agree the next step with the prescriber before the following dose.

The correct action depends on the injection and how much time has passed, so check its instructions or contact the prescriber or pharmacist. Do not take two doses together or guess a new schedule.

An option may be suitable, or it may not be, depending on the diagnosis, stability of the condition, current blood pressure and other medicines. Do not start before a clinician reviews the full list. Chest pain, breathlessness or marked palpitations needs prompt assessment, not a new medicine.

A waist tape reflects abdominal fat better than a standard scale; scales measure total mass including water, muscle and bowel contents, so shrinking waist centimetres alongside stable weight usually means abdominal fat is falling, and a bioimpedance visceral fat score alone has limited accuracy [1, 7, 12].

Clinical consistency matters more than which protocol you select; the World Health Organization recommends the midpoint between the lower ribs and the pelvic crest, while many prefer the umbilicus as an easy home landmark; sticking to one site ensures reliable tracking [1, 9, 11].

It distorts the measurement significantly; sucking in your stomach can artificially shrink the reading within seconds, which is why you must stand relaxed, breathe normally and read the tape at the end of a gentle exhalation without holding your breath [8, 9].

Measuring once every two to four weeks is ideal; daily measurements capture fluid shifts and digestive contents after salty meals rather than true fat loss, whereas monthly trends reveal genuine metabolic change [6, 8, 9].

It is a simple calculation dividing waist circumference by height in matching units; clinical guidelines advise keeping the ratio below 0.5 (waist less than half your height) to minimize the risk of type 2 diabetes, hypertension and cardiovascular disease [4, 10].

If abdominal girth expands rapidly within days, or is accompanied by tight fluid distension, leg swelling, shortness of breath, intractable vomiting or jaundice, seek emergency medical evaluation to rule out ascites and hepatic or cardiovascular complications [3, 5, 7].

Very unlikely. Gaining 1.5 kilograms of true body fat takes a surplus in the region of 10,000 calories above your needs, which is very hard to reach in one evening meal. The overnight spike reflects temporary extracellular water retention provoked by dietary sodium, combined with the physical mass of food traversing your digestive tract [3, 8, 10].

The optimal time is first thing in the morning, immediately after waking and emptying your bladder, before consuming any fluids or food. Weigh yourself in minimal light clothing with your scale placed on a hard, level floor rather than carpet. An evening weigh-in is usually higher because of the day's food and fluids [11, 12].

No. Keep drinking plain water as usual; your kidneys need enough water to remove wastes and extra salts in urine. Cutting water out of fear of the scale will not clear the retained water faster. If you have heart or kidney disease and your doctor has set a fluid limit, follow that advice [7, 9].

This is medically unsafe and strictly discouraged without specialist supervision. Non-prescribed diuretics and herbal laxative teas deplete circulating intravascular fluid and vital electrolytes, creating risks of orthostatic dizziness, dangerous hypokalemia, and rebound water retention once the effect wears off [3, 7].

Benign post-meal fluid shifts are subtle, generalized, transient, and resolve on their own within a few days without localized discomfort. In contrast, pathologic swelling forms a lasting pitted indentation under pressure, persists for days, affects only one limb with heat and tenderness, or pairs with exertional shortness of breath [4, 5, 6, 9, 14].

Both approaches are used in research, and the right choice depends on your psychological relationship with the scale. Daily tracking is highly effective if you compute weekly rolling averages and remain unaffected by daily fluctuations. However, if daily numbers provoke anxiety or restrictive tendencies, weighing once weekly under consistent conditions is much healthier [11, 12].

Yes, it is possible. BMI does not show fat distribution, and fat concentrated around the abdomen is linked with metabolic risk even at a BMI that looks normal. This is why NICE recommends measuring waist-to-height ratio and uses lower thresholds for people of Middle Eastern background [2, 7].

According to the 2025 Lancet Commission, it is a condition in which excess fat is already affecting the function of an organ, such as the heart, liver, joints or breathing, or limiting basic daily activities. It needs active treatment rather than prevention alone [4].

Measure your waist with a tape halfway between the lowest rib and the top of the hip bone, at the end of a normal breath out, then divide by your height in the same unit. A result of 0.5 or more is a good reason to discuss risk with a clinician [2, 7].

Not necessarily. Relatively modest weight loss can improve blood pressure, glucose and other risk factors in many people. What matters is setting the goal around your health problem and measuring it with markers such as waist, blood tests, sleep and movement, not only the scale [5, 11].

Yes. Guidelines encourage asking permission before discussing weight and using respectful language. You can agree with your clinician when a measurement is genuinely useful and when it can wait, as long as it does not affect an important medical decision [1, 3, 8].

No. An assessment may lead to a nutrition and activity plan, follow-up, treatment of a related condition, or a discussion of medicine or surgery if suitable. Medicine is decided according to BMI, health status, benefits, harms and your choice [12, 14].

No fixed equivalence exists. Medicine response varies by drug, person and continuation, while sleeve gastrectomy is a surgical change with different benefits, risks and long-term commitments. Compare them for your health, complications and goals, not an advertised number or somebody else’s experience [5, 10, 13].

Do not start weight-management medicine by yourself. A clinician needs to review conditions, medicines, pregnancy or plans for it and contraindications, then select tests that your case requires. An unknown source or another person’s dose increases the risks of counterfeit product, dosing error and delayed response to adverse symptoms [5, 8, 9].

Not everyone regains the same amount, but regain is common and documented after stopping some medicines. Hunger signalling and the chronic disease can re-emerge; this is not weak willpower. Discuss treatment duration, maintenance and how any stop or switch will be supervised from the outset [5, 10].

No. The endoscopic procedure places internal sutures through the mouth to reduce stomach volume, whereas surgical sleeve gastrectomy removes part of the stomach.
