Instead, consult your treating clinician; clinical guidelines permit the temporary use of short-acting antacids or histamine-2 receptor antagonists (H2 blockers like famotidine), which do not alter bacterial urease activity and typically require only a 24 to 48 hour pause before the test [6, 8, 9, 10].

If a follow-up test demonstrates persistent H. pylori, standard clinical practice strictly prohibits repeating the initial antibiotic regimen, as the surviving strain has likely developed resistance [6, 7, 8]. The gastroenterologist prescribes an alternative salvage regimen—typically bismuth quadruple therapy or combinations featuring different antibiotics such as levofloxacin or tetracycline—with strict adherence required, followed by another full washout and repeat test of cure to verify eradication [1, 3, 6, 7, 8].

True reinfection rates after documented complete eradication are relatively low in adult populations (generally below 2% to 3% annually in clinical studies); most recurrences within the first year represent recrudescence of suppressed initial infection rather than a de novo infection [6, 7, 13, 14]. Preventive measures include rigorous hand hygiene with soap and water before meals and after bathroom use, drinking safe treated water, ensuring foods are thoroughly cooked and cleanly prepared, and avoiding sharing eating utensils with individuals experiencing active digestive symptoms [6, 7, 13, 14].

Not necessarily. Fatty liver is one possible cause, but ALT can rise for other reasons, and its level alone does not establish fat or fibrosis. A clinician interprets it with risk factors, the rest of the panel and symptoms, and may choose imaging or further assessment when context supports it. [3, 4, 5]

No. A normal panel is reassuring in many settings, but it does not exclude every condition or every degree of fibrosis. Meaning depends on why it was ordered, symptoms, risk factors and examination; the clinician decides whether it is sufficient or another assessment is appropriate. [1, 3, 5, 6]

Not every liver panel requires fasting, although it may be requested because of accompanying tests or specific instructions. Follow the directions for your own order and ask about water and medicines rather than fasting or withholding treatment independently. [2, 6]

Repeating can be useful, but timing depends on the degree and pattern of change, symptoms and likely cause. An unplanned repeat after a few days may capture variation without answering a clinical question. Ask what the repeat is intended to show and when it should be done. [2, 3, 4]

Yes. AST is also present in muscle, so muscle injury or strenuous activity near the test can affect interpretation. Do not assume exercise explains the result; report the timing and symptoms so the clinician can review the rest of the pattern. [2, 3, 4]

The number is interpreted in context, but new jaundice with severe pain, fever, repeated vomiting, confusion, bleeding, marked deterioration, dark urine or pale stool needs prompt assessment. Do not wait for a routine repeat when these warning signs are present. [1, 2, 8, 9]

Daily heartburn should not be ignored, but frequency alone does not establish the diagnosis or its cause. A clinician asks about regurgitation, duration, impact, medicine use, and features such as swallowing difficulty, bleeding or weight loss. Arrange assessment rather than continuing repeated self-treatment, and seek urgent help for new or severe chest pain. [1, 3, 4, 6]

No. Timing after food may fit reflux, but it does not exclude heart, lung or other causes. Do not use relief after an antacid as a home diagnostic test. New or severe chest pain, especially with breathlessness, cold sweating, dizziness or spreading pain, requires emergency help. [1, 5, 10]

Not everyone needs endoscopy. Typical symptoms without alarm features may begin with clinical assessment and a defined plan. Endoscopy is more useful when it answers a question, such as swallowing difficulty, possible bleeding or symptoms persisting despite an appropriate plan. The decision depends on your circumstances, and a normal endoscopy does not exclude every cause of symptoms. [3, 4, 8, 11]

Throat symptoms and cough can occur with reflux in some people, but they are not specific and have many possible causes. A clinician relates them to burning, regurgitation and timing while considering alternatives before attributing them to acid. Do not remain on prolonged acid treatment for cough without review. [1, 3, 7]

That depends on why the medicine was prescribed, its duration and dose, and whether inflammation or complications are present. Some plans are short and reviewed, while some conditions need longer treatment. Do not abruptly stop a prescribed medicine or change its dose yourself; ask how to reduce or continue safely and what to do if symptoms return. [3, 4, 12]

Not necessarily. Triggers vary, and broad restriction without a clear observation can be burdensome without benefit. Watch your own pattern, change one thing for a defined period and discuss the result at review. Large or late meals and lying down afterwards may matter more for one person, while a particular drink is clearer for another. [2, 6, 12]

No, do not stop any medication on your own. Essential blood pressure and cardiac medicines are generally taken as scheduled on procedure morning with a small sip of water, whereas diabetes medicines, anticoagulants, diuretics, and oral iron supplements require an individualized plan directed by your physician and the endoscopy team to safeguard against bleeding, dehydration, or hypoglycemia. [3, 6, 8, 9]

Bowel preparation is considered clinically adequate when your bowel output consists entirely of clear, pale yellow or light amber liquid without solid particles or dark debris, resembling clear urine or weak tea. If bowel movements remain cloudy, brown, or contain formed residue after finishing the solution, notify the endoscopy centre promptly so they can guide appropriate supplemental steps. [1, 2, 8, 10]

If severe nausea or vomiting develops, pause drinking the solution for 30 to 45 minutes to allow your stomach to settle, then resume slowly with small sips using a straw with the beverage well-chilled. If persistent vomiting prevents you from keeping fluids down, contact the endoscopy unit immediately so the team can advise on an anti-nausea remedy or adjust the regimen safely. [2, 5, 8, 10]

Red, purple, and dark dyes stain the colonic mucosal lining and discolor residual luminal fluid, mimicking blood and potentially confusing the examining physician into suspecting mucosal bleeding, inflammation, or vascular malformations, while obscuring small flat polyps. Stick exclusively to transparent or light-yellow fluids such as water, clear broth, and clarified apple juice. [1, 4, 5, 8]

No, you must not drive or travel home unaccompanied on public transit if you received sedation or anesthesia. Sedative agents impair judgment, concentration, and psychomotor reflexes for up to 24 hours, even if you feel alert upon waking. You must have a responsible adult escort accompany you from the unit and ensure you reach home safely. [1, 4, 5, 11]

Yes, chronic constipation slows colonic transit and increases the likelihood of inadequate preparation, which may compromise mucosal examination. Inform your clinician and the endoscopy centre well in advance, as they may recommend extending the low-residue diet by several days or incorporating a preparatory gentle laxative prior to the standard bowel-cleansing solution. [2, 8, 10]

Not necessarily. It is reassuring about what was seen and the question examined, but it does not judge the severity of a current symptom or exclude every cause. Severe or worsening pain or warning features need faster assessment. [1, 4, 10]

No. IBS is assessed from the symptom pattern, its relation to bowel movements and stool change, with history, examination and targeted tests when appropriate; it is not diagnosed from a normal scan alone. [7, 8]

Not automatically. The decision depends on the original question, whether visibility was limited, symptom changes, examination and other results. Review or a different test can sometimes be more appropriate than repetition. [1, 4]

Ultrasound is important when gallstones are the question, but a clinician reads it with the pain pattern, examination and blood tests. If symptoms change or the question differs, do not rely on an old report alone. [1, 5, 9]

Ultrasound may show some features in particular situations, but it cannot accurately stage fibrosis by itself or exclude fibrosis when those features are absent. A clinician selects suitable non-invasive assessment according to the question and risk. [1, 2, 5]

No. Liver tests are an important part of assessment but do not measure scarring alone. They are read with risk factors, earlier results and suitable assessment tools. [1, 3, 6]

Not necessarily. The decision depends on the reason for the appearance, symptoms, tests and risk factors, and whether the test will answer a question that changes the plan. [1, 2, 4]

No. They are different descriptions: fat accumulates in liver cells, while fibrosis is scarring. They may coexist, but one cannot be inferred from the other from a single report. [1, 2, 3]

Bring the ultrasound report, earlier tests with their dates, a list of every medicine, supplement and herbal product, and a note of any symptoms. This helps the clinician decide whether a risk estimate, another test or follow-up alone is needed. [1, 6, 8]

No. Bloating is common and can relate to gas, constipation, bowel motility and many other causes. H. pylori is confirmed with an appropriate test when the clinical history justifies the question, not from one symptom or the appearance of the abdomen. [1, 4, 10]

Not by itself. A response can be useful information, but different symptoms may improve temporarily with acid suppression. Diagnosis comes from the pattern, history and warning features, with selected tests when the pattern is unclear or treatment has not helped. [2, 5, 7]

They are different conditions and can coexist without one explaining every symptom of another. Confirming H. pylori does not prove that burning is reflux and does not diagnose IBS. A clinician connects each symptom cluster to its own pattern and appropriate assessment. [1, 2, 3, 8]

No. Ultrasound is useful for questions about organs such as the liver, gallbladder and kidneys, but it does not establish H. pylori, reflux or IBS. Each possibility has a different assessment pathway, and a clinician selects a test when its result could change the decision. [2, 4, 6, 9]

Some guidance requires a period without proton-pump inhibitors before a breath or stool-antigen test, while antibiotics and bismuth have different timing. Do not stop any medicine independently; the test type and your circumstances determine the instructions, so obtain them from the clinician or laboratory. [1, 4, 7]

No. Symptoms of disorders of gut–brain interaction are real, and stress may change their intensity in some people without replacing medical assessment or making them imaginary. Record the relationship if you notice it, but do not use it to dismiss a new change or warning feature. [3, 6, 8, 9]

Very possibly. Antibody levels can start dropping relatively quickly once gluten intake is reduced, which makes the test result less reliable [3, 4]. Tell the clinician exactly when you cut back and by how much, so they can decide whether the current test is sufficient or a supervised gluten-reintroduction period is needed before testing.

Not necessarily. If gluten was reduced before testing, or you have selective IgA deficiency, the result can be falsely negative [4]. The updated American guideline notes that persistent clinical suspicion despite a negative test warrants further evaluation by a gastroenterologist, rather than ruling out the diagnosis from a single test [2].

Yes. Mild or atypical symptoms, such as chronic fatigue or anaemia without obvious digestive complaints, are common in coeliac disease and can resemble other conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome or H. pylori infection [2]. A structured assessment by a specialist is the only reliable way to tell these apart before changing your diet.

The usual start is tTG-IgA with total IgA while you are eating gluten. If you have IgA deficiency or another relevant circumstance, the clinician selects an appropriate IgG test. Avoid ordering and interpreting a random panel on your own [1, 7].

No. Absence of HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 makes the disease very unlikely, but carrying either is common and does not establish diagnosis. Genetic testing helps in selected unclear situations [2, 7].

Do not start before gastroenterology review. Adults usually need endoscopy and biopsies to confirm diagnosis, and beginning the diet first can reduce the changes the clinician needs to see [1, 2].

No. ALT and AST may be normal or near normal despite steatosis and even clinically important fibrosis in some people. They are interpreted with platelets, history, imaging and fibrosis scores or tests, not alone [1, 6].

Routine ultrasound may show features of steatosis, but it is less sensitive for mild fat and cannot confirm inflammation or measure fibrosis accurately. The result may need FIB-4 or liver-stiffness testing according to clinical judgement [1, 6, 7].

Yes. Excess weight is a common risk factor but is not required. Glucose, blood lipids, blood pressure, fat distribution, genes, medicines and other causes may contribute, so assessment does not rely on the scale alone [2, 3, 12].

When excess weight is present, gradual loss can reduce liver fat and may improve inflammation and fibrosis to different degrees; activity helps even without major weight loss. Response depends on stage, so scarring should not be promised to disappear within a fixed period [4, 6, 9].

No. There is no proven detox that cleanses the liver, and some herbs or supplements can cause injury or interact with treatment. Show every product and dose to the clinician before starting or stopping it [4, 6, 11].

There is no single schedule for everyone. Timing depends on fibrosis probability, diabetes and other risks, prior results and the test used. Follow-up may repeat a score or stiffness test rather than automatically repeating ultrasound, so the clinician should set the interval [2, 6, 8, 10].

No. Blood antibody tests (IgG) cannot distinguish between an active current infection and a past exposure that has resolved, because circulating antibodies remain in the bloodstream for months or years after bacterial clearance. Clinical practice guidelines recommend active infection tests such as the urea breath test or stool antigen test, and advise against using blood serology to monitor treatment success [6, 7, 8].

Not necessarily. Bloating alone does not prove treatment failure, just as symptom relief alone does not prove bacterial eradication. The gastric lining requires time to heal from chronic inflammation, antibiotics can temporarily disrupt the gut microbiome, or an overlapping condition like functional dyspepsia or irritable bowel syndrome may coexist. Confirmation requires an objective test of cure at the correct time [5, 7, 8].

Because proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) suppress bacterial load and urease activity, while antibiotics and bismuth compounds diminish bacterial numbers in the stomach lining, which can produce a false-negative result on breath or stool tests despite active infection. Guidelines recommend stopping PPIs for at least 2 weeks and antibiotics or bismuth for at least 4 weeks before testing, under medical supervision [6, 7, 8].

No. Younger patients with uncomplicated dyspeptic symptoms and no warning signs typically begin with non-invasive tests such as the urea breath test or stool antigen test. A gastroscopy becomes necessary when alarm features appear, such as vomiting blood, black stools, difficulty swallowing, unexplained weight loss, anemia, or new-onset dyspepsia at an age or risk level for which local guidance advises endoscopy [1, 5, 9].

No. A positive active-infection result needs clinical review to confirm that testing conditions were appropriate, check allergies and previous antibiotic exposure, select a suitable regimen and plan the post-treatment test of cure. Repeating an old prescription or using someone else's treatment can fail and promote antimicrobial resistance [6, 7, 10].

No food, drink or herbal mixture has been shown to eradicate active infection in place of combination drug therapy. Dietary changes may ease a symptom for some people, but they neither test for nor eliminate the bacterium. Discuss supplements or herbs with the clinician because of possible interactions, and keep treatment and confirmation of cure medically supervised [3, 5, 6, 7].

Occasional transient bloating is a normal physiological occurrence that commonly follows large meals, carbonated beverages, or gas-producing legumes, resolving spontaneously within several hours once digestion occurs and gas or stool is passed [1, 4, 9]. In contrast, persistent bloating recurs multiple days per week, lasts for consecutive weeks or months, and often intensifies throughout the day with visible distension or altered bowel habits [4, 5, 10]. This ongoing pattern warrants formal medical evaluation by a gastroenterologist to identify underlying motility issues, constipation, irritable bowel syndrome, or other organic causes [5, 10].

You should not initiate an unsupervised restrictive diet or stop eating gluten simply because of persistent bloating. Eliminating dietary gluten prior to completing formal medical investigations causes antibody levels to decline rapidly, potentially producing falsely reassuring negative results on coeliac serology and delaying an accurate diagnosis [7, 8]. Furthermore, broadly eliminating entire food groups without professional oversight risks nutritional deficiencies and complicates identifying the true trigger [7, 13]. The proper step is keeping a brief symptom and food log to review with a gastroenterologist, who can guide targeted testing and supervise structured, temporary dietary trials if clinically indicated [3, 7, 8, 13].

Updated UK clinical guidance (NICE NG12) clarifies that persistent or frequent abdominal distension alone (particularly more than 12 times per month) is an individual symptom that warrants medical assessment without requiring coexisting symptoms [6]. The guideline specifies age-dependent pathways: measuring serum CA125 for women aged 40 and over (with ultrasound guided by age-specific CA125 thresholds), while advising against using CA125 in isolation for women aged 39 or under in favor of direct ultrasound, alongside heightened vigilance for women aged 50 and over presenting with new IBS-like symptoms where first-time IBS is rare [6, 7]. The treating clinician determines the appropriate work-up based on comprehensive evaluation, ordering pelvic ultrasound or CA125 as clinically indicated without unwarranted alarm [6, 9, 10].

Direct-to-consumer food sensitivity panels measuring IgG antibodies are not recommended for investigating bloating or gastrointestinal symptoms. Clinical guidelines from allergy and gastroenterology societies note that circulating IgG antibodies commonly reflect physiological exposure rather than intolerance or disease [5, 10, 13, 14]. Relying on these unvalidated commercial panels frequently prompts unwarranted, highly restrictive diets that cause nutritional deficits without treating the underlying gut disorder; clinical management relies instead on history, objective evaluation of motility, targeted diagnostic tests, and guided dietary adjustments [2, 5, 10, 13].

No. Persistent bloating does not automatically require imaging or endoscopy. Assessment usually starts with the symptom pattern, its relationship to meals and bowel movements, medicines, and an abdominal examination; the clinician then selects tests according to age, the clinical pattern, and any alarm features [2, 4, 9]. Ultrasound may be useful when the history or examination points toward an abdominal or pelvic-organ problem, while endoscopy needs a specific clinical indication rather than gas alone. Decisions are individual, so avoid arranging random tests or delaying assessment when there is weight loss, bleeding, persistent vomiting, severe pain, or progressive distension [2, 4, 6, 9].

No. Gastrointestinal symptoms may worsen around menstruation in women with or without IBS. Diagnosis depends on recurrent pain related to bowel movements and a change in stool form or frequency, considered alongside other findings. Marked pelvic pain, pain with bowel movements during periods, heavy bleeding or pain during sex also deserves discussion of a gynaecological cause [2, 8, 9].

IBS is a disorder of gut-brain interaction and has no specific structural sign on ultrasound or colonoscopy. Diagnosis rests on the symptom pattern and examination, with selected tests used when needed to assess alternatives. Ultrasound or endoscopy may be appropriate for a different question or a warning sign, but a normal result alone neither proves nor excludes IBS [1, 3, 5].

Do not stop gluten before assessment for coeliac disease because avoidance can alter test results. For dairy, record the relationship and amount rather than immediately excluding an entire food group. A clinician or dietitian can decide whether testing or a structured elimination and reintroduction is appropriate, avoiding unnecessary restriction or loss of a useful diagnostic clue [7, 11].

There is no single test panel for everyone. History, examination, age, the constipation or diarrhoea pattern, and warning signs determine what is useful. Some guidelines advise a full blood count, inflammatory markers and coeliac serology; a stool inflammatory marker may suit some people with diarrhoea. Endoscopy, imaging and breath tests need a specific indication and are not routine for every case [3, 5, 6].

IBS is not imaginary or a sign of psychological weakness. It is a complex disorder of gut-brain interaction. Stress or anxiety may amplify sensation and bowel activity for some people, while persistent symptoms can themselves increase anxiety. Treatment may combine digestive, dietary and gut-brain approaches according to individual needs [1, 2, 4, 6].

New persistent or frequent bloating with early satiety, reduced appetite, pelvic or abdominal pain, or urinary urgency and frequency warrants assessment, especially if an IBS-like pattern first appears after age 50. Bleeding, weight loss, anaemia, repeated vomiting or severe escalating pain requires faster assessment, and a severe emergency should not wait for a routine appointment [3, 10, 12].

The core pattern is the same: recurrent abdominal pain or discomfort related to defecation and a change in stool form or frequency. Symptoms and triggers can vary between individuals, but sex alone neither diagnoses IBS nor cancels warning signs. The clinician assesses your own history, not a separate male checklist [1, 2, 3].

A small amount of whitish mucus can occur with IBS. Red blood, blood mixed with stool, or black stool should not be attributed to IBS without assessment; seek urgent help if bleeding is heavy or accompanied by dizziness or fainting [1, 2, 9].

No. IBS is a genuine disorder of gut–brain interaction. Stress can alter gut sensitivity and movement in some people, while symptoms themselves may increase anxiety. Discussing sleep and stress is one part of complete care, not an accusation or a substitute for checking warning signs [1, 5, 10].

No. Colonoscopy does not prove IBS and may be unnecessary when the pattern is clear and alarm features are absent. It may be appropriate because of bleeding, anaemia, weight loss, family history, a test result or due colorectal screening. The decision is individual [2, 5, 6].

Preferably not, especially if your diet is already narrow or you are losing weight. It is a structured, time-limited trial followed by reintroduction and personalisation, not permanent restriction. A dietitian can protect nutritional adequacy and decide whether it fits. Do not remove gluten before discussing planned coeliac testing [11, 12].

Seek urgent care for sudden severe pain; a swollen abdomen with repeated vomiting or inability to pass stool and gas; heavy bleeding; black stool with weakness; fainting, confusion or breathing difficulty; or inability to keep fluids down. Do not try to prove it is an IBS flare when the condition is rapidly worsening [7, 9].

No. IBS can cause severe pain through altered gut sensitivity and motility, but it does not cause visible digestive-tract damage or “turn into” cancer. However, very new or different pain, especially with bleeding, weight loss, fever, vomiting or fainting, should not be attributed to IBS without assessment [1, 2, 3].

Blood is not a typical IBS symptom. It has both minor and more important causes, but colour, amount and accompanying symptoms cannot establish the cause at home. Seek prompt assessment for any bleeding, and urgent care for heavy bleeding, black tarry stool, dizziness, fainting, breathlessness or marked weakness [3, 8, 9].

Not every case. Colonoscopy depends on alarm features, age, family history, examination, laboratory results and relevant screening programmes, not pain intensity alone. Some cases can be diagnosed from a positive symptom pattern with limited tests, whereas bleeding, anaemia, weight loss or an abnormal result may change the decision. The treating clinician determines its value and timing [3, 5, 6, 11].

Do not stop gluten before coeliac testing on your own because this can alter test accuracy. For dairy or any food group, record the relationship to symptoms and discuss a structured trial rather than removing many foods at once. Broad restriction can create nutritional problems and make the true trigger harder to identify [6, 7, 12].

IBS is a real disorder of gut-brain interaction, with food, prior infection and stress contributing differently between people. Stress can amplify gut sensitivity and a flare, but it does not make pain imaginary. Care may combine dietary change, medicine, sleep, activity and gut-directed psychological therapy according to individual need [1, 2, 4, 7].

Bring a short timeline, stool frequency and form, a medicine and supplement list, previous results, and any family history of coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease or colorectal cancer. Clearly mention bleeding, fever, weight loss, night symptoms, travel and antibiotic exposure. This information helps the clinician choose targeted investigation rather than random testing [3, 5, 7].

Yes. Liver fat and metabolic factors can improve with sustained changes in food and activity, gradual weight loss when appropriate, and management of glucose, lipids and blood pressure. The degree and timing differ between people, while fibrosis changes the goals and follow-up. Do not judge progress by one symptom or an early ultrasound; agree on measures and a review point with the clinician [3, 4, 5].

Not necessarily. ALT and AST can be normal despite steatosis or clinically important fibrosis, and lower values alone do not prove that all liver injury has resolved. The clinician reads the trend alongside platelets, glucose and weight factors, fibrosis-risk results and appropriate imaging. Follow-up is reduced or continued according to overall risk, not one enzyme value [2, 4, 6].

Usually not. Routine ultrasound can identify the appearance of liver fat and some structural changes, but it is not a precise measure of small changes and cannot establish inflammation or fibrosis stage. Repeat timing depends on the clinical question, findings and risk, while follow-up may rely more on metabolic measures, targeted blood tests and repeat fibrosis assessment. Avoid repeating imaging only for reassurance when there is no plan for using the result [2, 4, 6].

Not everyone needs a weight-loss target. Fatty liver can occur at a weight within the usual range, so the clinician reviews waist distribution, food quality, activity, glucose, lipids and other causes. The goal may be better meal composition and fitness with less abdominal fat while preserving muscle, rather than pursuing a lower number on the scale. The plan should be individualised [4, 5].

No. The body needs appropriate dietary fats, and care generally focuses on the quality of the whole eating pattern and limiting added sugars, sugary drinks and highly processed food, not eliminating all fat. Detox mixtures have not been shown to remove liver fat, and some herbs and supplements are linked to liver injury. Review any product with a clinician or pharmacist before using it [3, 4, 10].

No. Medicines for associated diabetes or obesity are selected when there is an appropriate indication. The targeted medicine resmetirom has FDA approval for a defined group of adults with noncirrhotic MASH and moderate-to-advanced fibrosis, not for everyone with steatosis. Stage, interactions, local availability and monitoring must be assessed by a specialist [5, 9].

No. Many infected people have no symptoms, while some develop gastritis or an ulcer with upper-abdominal pain, early fullness or nausea. The presence or absence of symptoms cannot establish infection; testing is chosen according to the clinical reason and context [1, 2, 7].

No single test is best in every situation. Urea breath and stool antigen tests are strong options for active infection, while biopsy testing fits when endoscopy is required for another reason. Accuracy also depends on preparation, medicine timing and laboratory method, so the clinician matches the test to the question [1, 3, 8].

Not necessarily. Antibody tests can remain positive after an old infection and cannot show whether H. pylori is active now or has cleared after treatment. Show the report to a clinician; a breath or stool test may be needed to establish active infection instead of starting antibiotics from an incomplete result [1, 4, 8].

Many guidelines require two weeks off a proton-pump inhibitor before breath or stool testing and four weeks after antibiotics or bismuth, especially for proof of cure. Do not stop essential treatment yourself; the medicine, your condition and the laboratory protocol may alter the plan, and a clinician can advise a temporary alternative when appropriate [5, 6, 8].

No. Symptoms may improve while infection persists, or continue after successful eradication because another problem is present. Cure should be confirmed with a correctly timed breath or stool antigen test, or a biopsy-based test if endoscopy is independently indicated. Blood antibody testing cannot prove cure [1, 5, 6].

Do not repeat the same prescription yourself. The clinician reviews the medicines, doses, adherence, adverse effects and every antibiotic used previously, then chooses a different regimen or susceptibility testing where available. Antibiotic resistance is an important cause of failure, and blindly repeating the same combination can reduce the chance of success [6, 11, 12].

Once the endoscopy unit allows food and you are properly awake, start with a small amount of familiar food that is easy for you, such as light soup, plain rice or potato, bread, eggs, or a light protein. There is no compulsory universal menu; return to your usual diet depends on tolerance and whether a biopsy or polyp removal occurred. If you feel nauseated, eat slowly and delay a large or fatty meal. Your own discharge instructions remain the reference. [1, 3, 4, 5, 6]

Gas and mild intermittent cramps are common because air or carbon dioxide is used during the examination. Improvement commonly begins within hours, although mild symptoms may extend through the first day according to the unit’s advice. The key is improvement, not escalation. Marked or increasing swelling, a rigid abdomen, severe or persistent pain, fever or vomiting requires urgent contact and assessment according to severity. [1, 2, 5, 6, 8, 11]

Mild cramps that come and go and improve after passing gas can be expected. Severe, constant or worsening pain, or pain that prevents movement or sleep, should not automatically be labelled as gas. If pain comes with marked swelling, fever, vomiting, bleeding, dizziness or general deterioration, seek urgent assessment and take the report with you. Do not start a new pain medicine independently after biopsy or polyp removal before asking the team. [2, 3, 6, 8, 11]

A spot or small amount of blood may occur after biopsy or polyp removal, and the unit will usually give a specific observation period. A large amount, clots, bleeding that increases or continues, black tarry stool, dizziness or weakness needs urgent contact. Bleeding after polyp removal can be delayed, so always state the date of colonoscopy and the intervention performed, and do not replace your discharge sheet with generic advice. [1, 2, 6, 7, 9, 13]

If you received sedation, many instructions prohibit driving, machinery, alcohol and important decisions for 24 hours and require an escort home. Follow your unit’s period because it relates to the medicine used, and do not treat feeling awake as proof that driving is safe. Return to work or exercise also depends on biopsy or polyp removal and the activity involved, so check the written instructions. [2, 4, 5, 6, 7]

Warning signs include severe or worsening abdominal pain, marked swelling or a rigid abdomen, heavy or increasing bleeding, clots or black stool, fever or chills, repeated vomiting, inability to drink, fainting or marked dizziness and weakness, confusion, or breathlessness. Contact the endoscopy unit immediately or go to emergency care according to severity; do not wait for a clinic appointment or drive yourself if you are unstable. [2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11]

It is a thin, flexible tube introduced through the anus and guided through the rectum and colon so the clinician can inspect the lining. Colonoscopy does not enter through the mouth; that is the gastroscopy route. Small instruments can pass through the scope for a biopsy or polyp removal when indicated and consented. [1, 5, 6]

Experiences vary. You may feel fullness, pressure or cramps as the colon expands and the scope passes bends, and some people need more analgesia or sedation. Nobody can accurately promise that you will feel nothing. Agree how to alert the team before starting and speak up if pain increases so they can assess and adjust the plan when needed. [2, 5, 7]

Not necessarily. Options differ by centre and situation and may include no sedative, gas or analgesia, or intravenous sedation at different depths. Moderate sedation is not general anaesthesia, and you may remain able to respond while drowsy. Ask what is available to you and what monitoring and escort are required; the team makes the final choice after assessing your health. [2, 7, 8]

Patient resources commonly describe roughly 30 to 60 minutes for the examination itself, but this is neither fixed nor a discharge time. Washing, ease of passage, biopsies, polyp removal and other treatment can alter it. The whole visit is longer because of registration, preparation, consent, recovery and discharge instructions, so ask your centre for an approximate window and keep the day flexible. [1, 2, 5]

It depends on the centre’s plan and the sedation depth suitable for you. Without a sedative you are awake; with light or moderate sedation you may be awake but relaxed or drowsy and able to respond, and may not remember every detail. Deeper sedation has different monitoring requirements. Do not assume that “anaesthetic” means complete unconsciousness; ask for the plan’s name and expected effect. [7, 8]

Follow your discharge sheet and seek urgent help according to severity for severe or worsening pain, fever, repeated vomiting, heavy or persistent bleeding, black stool, marked distension that is not improving, fainting, breathing difficulty, chest pain or clear deterioration. Mild cramps and gas can occur, but your intervention and health change how symptoms are interpreted, so contacting the centre is safer than guessing. [1, 3, 5, 6]

It describes a projection seen from the gallbladder wall into its cavity, not a tissue diagnosis. Many small projections are benign cholesterol deposits or polyp mimics, and ordinary ultrasound can produce false-positive findings. Its practical meaning depends on size, morphology, movement, shadowing, wall thickness, clinical context and sometimes comparison with a later scan—not on the word “polyp” alone [1, 3, 4].

A typical polyp is attached to the wall, remains fixed when position changes and has no posterior acoustic shadow, whereas a stone usually moves and casts a shadow. Tiny impacted stones and clumped sludge can still mimic a polyp, and both findings can coexist. The complete report and images therefore need review, including measurements and morphology, rather than self-diagnosis from one feature [3, 4].

Under the European guideline, a polyp of 5 mm or less without specified risk factors needs no surveillance, while the same size with a risk factor may enter planned ultrasound follow-up. Other frameworks, including SRU and Korean recommendations, classify lesions differently by morphology and context. The number alone cannot set your plan; age, PSC, shape, wall thickness and scan quality need clinical review [1, 2, 3].

There is no single interval for every case. As one example, the European pathway scans selected lesions at 6 months, 1 year and 2 years, stopping if there is no growth; very small low-risk lesions need no surveillance, while others prompt surgical discussion. SRU and other systems use different schedules. Ask your clinician to document the interval, reason, stopping point and guideline used [1, 2, 3, 12].

No. A small increase may reflect natural growth or measurement variation, and follow-up studies record enlargement in some polyps and shrinkage or disappearance in others. With growth of 2 mm or more within 2 years, the European guideline calls for reassessment of current size alongside risk factors; it does not label that number alone as cancer. Proper comparison needs the dates, measurements and morphology from both scans [1, 7, 8].

Surgery is not based on the word “polyp” alone. The European guideline discusses removal at 10 mm or above in a person fit for surgery, for some 6–9 mm lesions with specified risk factors, or for potentially gallbladder-related symptoms after excluding another cause. Other guidance uses different morphology-based thresholds, and PSC needs specialist input. The final decision includes image review, benefits, risks and your preferences [1, 2, 11, 12].

It is a mixture of tiny crystals, mucus and bile components that appears on ultrasound as dependent bright material, usually without a clear acoustic shadow. It is an imaging description, not proof by itself of inflammation or a need for treatment; symptoms and the rest of the gallbladder and duct findings determine its importance [1, 2].

Not exactly. Sludge is fine material that usually layers or clumps without shadowing, while a stone is a defined bright object that commonly shadows and moves with position. Tiny stones can be difficult to separate from sludge, which is why some reports reasonably state both possibilities [1, 2, 10].

Not all sludge is dangerous, but it should not be interpreted without context. It may disappear or remain quiet, and in some cases it is associated with stones, inflammation, obstruction or pancreatitis. Risk is assessed from symptoms, blood tests, the gallbladder wall and bile ducts, not from the report word alone [1, 4, 11].

Not automatically. An incidental report without compatible symptoms or complications is not a ready-made operation decision. Surgical discussion becomes more relevant with convincing biliary attacks, inflammation, obstruction or pancreatitis, after symptoms are correlated with examination, blood tests and imaging [6, 8, 11].

There is no fixed interval for everyone. A clinician may repeat the scan when the first examination was unclear, symptoms persist or change, a temporary driver needs follow-up, or a new result would alter management. When sludge is entirely incidental, follow-up is individualised rather than repeated without a clinical purpose [1, 6, 11].

Yes. No examination guarantees detection of every tiny stone, and bowel gas, preparation, stone location and size can limit the view. If symptoms and tests still suggest a duct stone despite ultrasound, a clinician may discuss MRCP or EUS according to the details rather than ordering them for everyone [1, 5, 6].

The actual procedural time within the endoscopy room typically spans 25 to 45 minutes for both scopes combined [1, 2, 6]. Upper endoscopy generally takes 7 to 12 minutes, while colonoscopy requires 15 to 30 minutes depending on anatomical navigation and therapeutic polypectomy [1, 2, 6]. Total time spent at the endoscopy center generally totals 2 to 3 hours, covering admission checks, anesthesia preparation, and post-procedure recovery monitoring [3, 4, 9].

Patients do not experience pain during the combined examination under modern intravenous sedation managed by clinical professionals [9, 10]. Sedative medications induce deep relaxation or light-to-moderate sleep, effectively abolishing pharyngeal gagging during upper endoscopy and blunting colonic pressure sensations [9, 10]. Upon awakening, sensations are generally limited to mild transient throat dryness or gaseous distension that resolves within a few hours [1, 3, 4, 11].

Extensive clinical literature confirms that same-day bidirectional endoscopy is thoroughly safe, with adverse event rates comparable to scheduling the procedures across separate visits [6, 9, 11]. Combining the procedures provides the notable safety advantage of exposing the body to a single session of sedation rather than two, while sparing the patient repeat bowel cleanses and fasts [6, 10].

Precise coordination relies on a split-dose preparation regimen, where the first dose is taken the evening prior and the second dose early on the procedure morning, roughly 4 to 6 hours before check-in [9, 13]. The mandatory safety rule is to stop all fluid and prep consumption at least 2 full hours prior to sedation, ensuring complete gastric emptying and pulmonary safety [9, 13].

Driving a motor vehicle, operating machinery, and returning to workplace duties are strictly forbidden on the day of the procedure following intravenous sedation [3, 4, 9]. Sedatives impair psychomotor reflexes and concentration for many hours after waking; an adult escort must accompany you home, and you should rest for the remainder of the day before resuming routine activity the next morning [3, 4, 9].

A normal endoscopic result is highly reassuring, definitively ruling out mucosal ulcers, severe active inflammation, polyps, or luminal malignancies along the evaluated tracts [1, 2, 7]. If symptoms persist, your gastroenterologist evaluates functional gut disorders such as IBS or visceral hypersensitivity, or considers targeted small-bowel investigations and metabolic lab panels to guide symptom management [7, 8].

Gastroscopy is performed with the patient resting comfortably on their left side as the slender endoscope is guided through the mouth into the oesophagus and stomach, and it does not cause suffocation because it travels through the alimentary tract, leaving the airway and trachea entirely unobstructed [1, 2, 3]. The patient breathes steadily and naturally through the nose and mouth throughout the examination, while the mouthguard and local throat spray ensure comfortable passage without impeding ventilation [1, 2, 3].

Gastroscopy is not sharply painful because the inner gastrointestinal lining lacks somatic pain receptors, causing instead temporary discomfort, mild gagging sensations, and gaseous fullness [1, 2, 3]. General anaesthesia is not routinely required; the procedure is successfully performed either with local anaesthetic throat spray alone with the patient alert, or with intravenous conscious sedation inducing restful relaxation, with the choice guided by patient health and individual preference [1, 2, 3, 12].

No, taking a mucosal biopsy during gastroscopy is a standard, routine diagnostic procedure and does not indicate cancer or a grave condition [1, 3, 12]. Tissue samples are obtained in the overwhelming majority of cases for benign purposes, such as identifying Helicobacter pylori infection, grading chronic gastritis, or ruling out celiac disease in the duodenum, with pathology results returning within several days to guide targeted medical care [1, 3, 6, 9, 11, 12].

You can begin drinking and eating once the local throat anaesthetic spray has completely worn off, which generally takes approximately forty-five to sixty minutes after the procedure [1, 2, 3]. Once normal swallowing sensation returns, you should take a small test sip of water; once swallowed comfortably, you can proceed to light, soft foods like broth or yogurt while avoiding heavy, spicy, or greasy meals for the rest of the day [1, 2, 12].

The active procedural time for a diagnostic gastroscopy typically spans just five to fifteen minutes, which provides sufficient time to inspect the oesophagus, stomach, and duodenum thoroughly and obtain any needed biopsies [1, 2, 3]. However, the total duration of the clinic visit ranges between one and two hours to accommodate pre-procedure preparation, baseline checks, and post-procedure recovery monitoring [1, 2, 3].

Local throat spray numbs only the pharyngeal mucosa to reduce the gag reflex while keeping the patient fully awake, allowing for immediate independent discharge [1, 2, 3]. Conversely, intravenous conscious sedation induces deep relaxation and temporary amnesia, eliminating procedure-related anxiety, but mandates an adult escort to accompany the patient home and strict avoidance of driving for twenty-four hours [1, 2, 3, 12].

Frequently asked questions

Abdominal Ultrasound

Yes, if you have a request from your own doctor. We perform the scan, you receive the report, and you take it back to them. If you have no doctor following you and you want an opinion on the symptoms themselves, a consultation suits you better: it includes the scan and reads it against your history and your labs.

Yes: six to eight hours beforehand, and water is fine. It also helps to avoid fizzy drinks and bloating foods the day before, because gas gets in the way of the image.

In the same visit. The doctor performs the scan and reads it with you in the room, so there is no report written up two days later by someone who never saw you.

We will tell you plainly and write it in the report. If it needs an opinion or a next step you can book a consultation here or take it back to your own doctor: the choice is yours, and the report is yours either way.

Ultrasound can show an appearance consistent with fat accumulation, but it cannot accurately measure inflammation or fibrosis by itself. The report is read with the history, examination and liver, glucose and lipid tests before deciding whether follow-up or another assessment is needed.

Not automatically. The change may be fat, fluid, medicine-related or hormonal, so symptoms and examination determine whether ultrasound would help and which area to assess. Clear swelling, breathlessness or chest pain needs prompt evaluation.

Routine abdominal ultrasound is not a comprehensive, precise measure of all visceral fat. It may show fatty liver or a particular problem, while abdominal-fat risk also uses waist size, blood pressure, glucose and blood lipids. Further imaging is selected only when it would change care.

Fasting is not identical across all pediatric age groups and depends strictly on the child's age and the specific organs being evaluated; infants under 2 years fast for only 2 to 3 hours (scheduling right before a regular milk feed), children aged 2 to 5 years fast for about 3 to 4 hours, and older children fast for 4 to 6 hours for upper abdominal exams [1, 3, 4, 15]. Small sips of water are permitted, and scans evaluating only the urinary tract or acute emergencies never require fasting [4, 12, 13].

A routine abdominal ultrasound evaluates upper and mid-abdominal organs such as the liver, gallbladder, spleen, pancreas, and kidneys, whereas a pelvic ultrasound assesses the urinary bladder, distal ureters, and deep pelvic reproductive organs such as the ovaries and uterus in girls [1, 4, 8, 12]. Pelvic imaging requires a comfortably full bladder to provide an acoustic window, and clinicians frequently perform both components together during a single comprehensive visit [1, 4, 8, 12].

Diagnostic ultrasound is 100% safe and involves zero ionising radiation; it functions entirely using harmless mechanical sound waves that reflect off internal tissues, making it completely safe for newborns, infants, and children of all ages, and it can be repeated as often as necessary without biological risks [1, 2, 4, 12].

Mild movement or crying is completely normal, expected, and anticipated by experienced paediatric ultrasound clinicians and does not invalidate the study; in fact, the deep inspiration a child takes during crying can temporarily lower the diaphragm and enhance visualization of the liver [1, 4, 13, 14]. Clinicians use soothing strategies—such as pacifiers, feeds, or favourite videos—and acquire diagnostic images patiently without rushing [1, 4, 13].

A normal ultrasound is reassuring news that firmly excludes acute surgical pathologies and structural lesions, but it does not mean the child's pain is imaginary, as ultrasound does not visualize functional motility changes, constipation, food intolerances, or superficial mucosal inflammation [4, 5, 8, 13]. The proper next step is clinical paediatric follow-up to address bowel patterns, diet, and functional pain management without repeating unnecessary scans [5, 8, 13].

Ultrasound is universally recognized as the preferred first-line imaging modality for paediatric appendicitis to spare children unnecessary CT radiation, carrying high diagnostic accuracy when the inflamed, non-compressible appendix is directly visualized [6, 13]. If overlying bowel gas obscures the appendix while clinical symptoms persist, management relies on clinical serial observation and surgical evaluation to safeguard the child's health [6, 13].

Abdominal ultrasound is not designed to evaluate the mucosal lining of the colon, because intraluminal gas and feces scatter sound waves and obscure the internal mucosal surface [6, 8, 10]. While ultrasound excels at evaluating solid organs such as the liver, gallbladder, and kidneys, and can occasionally identify secondary signs like gross wall thickening in acute inflammation or bulky masses, it cannot comprehensively assess the colon or rule out standard bowel disorders [8, 10, 12].

No. A normal abdominal ultrasound report absolutely does not exclude colon cancer or precancerous adenomatous polyps [1, 4, 9, 13]. A normal ultrasound simply indicates that the organs visualized well (such as the liver, kidneys, and spleen) demonstrated no macroscopic mass lesions, but it cannot visualize small polyps or early mucosal malignancies arising inside the colon lumen; relying on a normal scan to dismiss persistent symptoms is unsafe [4, 8, 9, 13].

Ultrasound can occasionally identify colon tumours only at relatively advanced stages, when a lesion becomes bulky, produces marked full-thickness wall thickening, or forms a conspicuous mass (such as the pseudokidney sign), or when complications arise such as bowel obstruction, hepatic metastases, or malignant ascites [7, 10, 11, 12, 13]. Early-stage malignancies and precancerous polyps that are most amenable to curative endoscopic treatment remain invisible on standard transabdominal imaging [9, 10, 13].

A colonoscopy is needed when clinical red flags indicate direct visualization of the bowel mucosa: visible rectal bleeding or blood in stool, unexplained iron deficiency anaemia, unexplained involuntary weight loss, or a persistent change in bowel habits lasting over 4 to 6 weeks in adults aged 45 to 50 and older, as well as significant family history of colorectal cancer [1, 2, 4, 7, 9]. Colonoscopy enables precise mucosal inspection, tissue biopsy, and immediate polyp removal in a single session [3, 5, 9].

No. Common abdominal cramps, bloating, or flatulence do not automatically justify an invasive colonoscopy; the vast majority of digestive complaints stem from functional disorders like irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), dietary patterns, or simple constipation, which are managed clinically once alarm symptoms are excluded [1, 4, 7, 9]. Colonoscopy involves targeted preparation and sedation, and is reserved for substantiated clinical indications [3, 5, 7, 9].

The guideline-endorsed non-invasive test for population-based colorectal cancer screening in asymptomatic average-risk adults is the quantitative Faecal Immunochemical Test (FIT) [2, 9]. This test detects microscopic traces of human hemoglobin in stool that cannot be seen with the naked eye; if positive, it prompts expedited diagnostic colonoscopy to locate the source and resect any detected polyps [1, 2, 4, 9].

A cyst confidently characterized as simple has a recognized benign appearance and usually causes no harm or need for treatment. The important point is that “simple” should be based on complete imaging features, not inferred from size or from the word cyst alone. If the description is indeterminate, includes septa or a solid component, or supplementary imaging is requested, the appropriate step is further characterization rather than assuming either a simple cyst or cancer [1, 2, 6].

No. Measurement alone does not determine the cyst’s nature or the treatment decision. The clinician reviews whether the appearance is genuinely simple, whether there is matching pain or pressure on urine drainage, whether kidney function is affected, and whether a real change exists compared with prior images. A large simple cyst may remain asymptomatic, while a smaller indeterminate lesion may need better imaging because of its appearance [1, 2, 4].

A confidently simple asymptomatic cyst usually does not need routine imaging surveillance, but do not cancel a documented plan before understanding its reason. Follow-up may have been requested because characterization was incomplete, a particular feature was present, no earlier images exist, or the kidney context differs. Ask about the examination’s purpose and which change would alter management rather than applying one schedule to every case [1, 4, 5, 6].

This can occur uncommonly if a cyst is large and compressive, infected, bleeding or ruptured, but most simple cysts cause no symptoms. Pain and haematuria have many other causes, including stones, infection and conditions elsewhere in the urinary tract, so they should not automatically be attributed to the cyst. Visible blood, fever with pain, or reduced urine output needs prompt assessment according to severity [1, 2, 11, 12].

A simple cyst is commonly solitary or one of a few that appear with age and usually does not alter kidney structure or function. Inherited PKD causes numerous cysts, may enlarge the kidneys and affect function, and assessment often considers family history, blood pressure and other organs. A report containing one cyst is not a diagnosis of inherited PKD; number, distribution, age and family history guide that question [1, 13].

No food or drink is known to dissolve a simple cyst. Do not force excessive water intake or stop medicines or food groups to try a home treatment, particularly if you have heart or kidney disease. A simple cyst causing no problem usually needs no treatment; when symptoms, obstruction or a non-simple appearance are present, management is a clinician-directed decision aimed at the actual issue [1, 2, 4].

Yes, drinking water to achieve adequate bladder filling is clinically indispensable because ultrasound sound waves cannot penetrate intestinal gas, which scatters and reflects acoustic beams [2, 5, 14]. A full bladder serves as an acoustic window that physically displaces bowel loops up and away from the pelvis, allowing the sound beam to clearly delineate the bladder wall, trigone, and the prostate gland located immediately beneath it [2, 5, 9, 10, 14].

Standard clinical protocols recommend drinking 3 to 4 glasses of plain water (approximately 750 ml to 1 litre), finished 45 to 60 minutes prior to your examination without voiding [2, 4, 7, 10]. You should never force down excessive volumes that trigger agonizing pain; the clinical target is a comfortably full bladder where you feel a distinct urge to void without acute distress or spasms [1, 2, 7, 10].

Yes, when upper abdominal organs are combined with pelvic evaluation, complete fasting from solid food for 6 hours is necessary so the gallbladder remains distended and upper intestinal gas is minimized [3, 5, 9, 11]. During this fasting period, drinking plain water during the hour prior to the scan is permitted to fill the bladder, while strictly avoiding juices, dairy, tea, gum, and smoking [5, 9, 11, 12].

This step measures the Post-Void Residual (PVR) urine volume, a cornerstone measurement for evaluating bladder emptying efficiency [1, 2, 7, 9, 10]. While a healthy bladder empties almost completely (leaving under 20 to 50 ml), significant residual urine indicates outflow impairment, resulting either from mechanical prostatic obstruction or weakened bladder detrusor contraction [1, 2, 7, 9, 10].

No, transabdominal ultrasound estimates gland volume and identifies urinary obstruction, but it cannot confirm or rule out prostate malignancy [1, 4, 7, 8, 9, 14]. Most enlargement visualized on ultrasound represents benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH); when malignancy is clinically suspected or PSA is elevated, multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) and targeted biopsy are required for diagnostic confirmation [4, 7, 8, 9, 14].

Prostatic calcifications (corpora amylacea) are benign mineral deposits found very commonly in adult men, reflecting physiological aging or prior resolved inflammation rather than malignancy [1, 4, 7, 10, 14]. The clinician reviews this incidental appearance alongside overall clinical symptoms without any cause for alarm [1, 4, 7, 10, 14, 15].

Frequently asked questions

General & Laparoscopic Surgery

No. Small, symptom-free hernias can sometimes be watched. But a hernia that is enlarging, painful, or causing obstruction needs intervention, and delaying raises the risk. The assessment distinguishes between the two.

It depends on the procedure and the approach. Laparoscopic operations generally return you to normal activity far faster than open surgery. The surgeon will give you the expected timeline for your specific case before the operation.

The consultation, the assessment and the post-operative follow-up take place at the clinic. The operations themselves are performed in an equipped hospital, and the surgeon will agree the details with you.

Not necessarily. Local fat or excess skin is different from obesity requiring surgery, and the choice depends on weight stability, area, skin, health and a realistic aim. Assessment can separate observation, a non-surgical option, specialist plastic-surgery advice or an operation.

The decision does not come from weight alone or one unsuccessful diet. A surgeon reviews BMI, related conditions, previous attempts, readiness for follow-up and risk, and explains alternatives. Assessment may lead to a non-surgical plan or the bariatric pathway.

There is no best option for everyone. The decision depends on severity, related illness, previous response, contraindications, your preference and ability to continue long-term follow-up. Compare benefits, risks and commitments with the weight-management and surgical teams.

In adults, no: a hernia does not heal by itself and surgery is the only way to repair it, although not every hernia needs an operation straight away. Umbilical hernias in babies are different, and many close on their own during early childhood. [1, 4, 5]

Not always. A man with an inguinal hernia and few symptoms may be offered watchful waiting after seeing a surgeon, while a femoral hernia is usually repaired because it carries a higher risk of complications. Any hernia that becomes painful, firm and stuck needs emergency care. [2, 6]

A hernia that slides back on its own when you lie down is common. Do not force a painful or firm bulge; if it will not go back and hurts, or you feel sick or cannot pass wind, go to the emergency department. [2, 5]

No. It may be a separation of the abdominal muscles, which often improves with time and physiotherapy exercises. A true umbilical or incisional hernia is also possible, so an examination is needed to tell them apart. [7, 10]

Often not. Many hernias are diagnosed by examination alone, while you stand and cough. Ultrasound, CT or MRI is used when the examination is unclear or when a complex repair is being planned. [1, 9, 10]

Not necessarily. Surgery is aimed at symptoms that come from gallstones, mainly biliary pain and complications. If the bloating has another cause it may continue after the operation, and the NHS notes that some people have ongoing digestive symptoms after gallbladder removal. [7, 10] Ask your surgeon which symptoms the operation is expected to help.

For stones in a normal gallbladder and bile ducts that cause no symptoms, NICE advises that treatment is not needed unless symptoms develop. [10] What matters is knowing the warning signs, such as severe or prolonged pain, fever, yellow eyes or skin and dark urine, and seeking care if they appear. [1]

Gallstone pain is usually a steady, severe pain in the upper right or upper middle abdomen that comes in attacks lasting minutes to hours, sometimes spreading to the back or right shoulder, often with nausea. [1, 2] Bloating is more a feeling of fullness, pressure or swelling that often varies with meals and gas. [11]

It depends on your symptoms and results. If the bile duct looks widened or liver tests are abnormal, NICE suggests an MRCP scan may be considered to look for a stone in the duct. [10] If the pattern points to another digestive cause, different tests, or none, may be more useful. [11]

Bring a short timeline of when the symptoms started and what makes them better or worse, a list of your medicines and supplements (especially blood thinners), and any previous operation reports, imaging or recent test results. This helps the clinician focus the history and examination and decide whether imaging is actually needed. [1, 10]

Go urgently if you have severe or prolonged abdominal pain, fever or shivering, yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine or pale stools, or vomiting that will not stop. [1, 2]

It is deliberate. The surgical safety checklist has pauses before anaesthesia, before the incision and before leaving the operating room, and each person confirms for themselves before the step they are responsible for. [1, 2]

The best-known study found fewer deaths and complications after it was introduced, and later reviews found improvement in many settings, but the effect depends on how it is used and is not the same everywhere. [3, 4, 8]

If the operation has a right and left side or a specific site, the mark helps the team confirm the correct place, and it is one of the safety items before anaesthesia. [1, 2]

Say so immediately and clearly, even if you answered before. The purpose of the pauses is that anyone, including you, can stop the step if something is not right. [1, 6]

No. It reduces avoidable errors and improves communication, but every operation has its own risks, which the surgeon explains before you give consent. [3, 4]

No. A stone alone is not enough; symptoms, complications and assessment results determine whether removal is appropriate.

Not necessarily. It can be an intentional safety decision when the details of the case make an open approach safer.

No. Ultrasound is important, but the surgeon combines it with symptoms, examination, blood results, health history and sometimes additional tests.

Follow the progression and team instructions, because food return depends on the procedure, tolerance and health situation. Do not rely on a general online list.

Bowel change can have several causes after surgery. If it persists or is severe, or comes with dehydration, pain or fever, contact the team for assessment in your context.

Do not increase or change medicine on your own. Increasing pain may require a question about the cause, and the team decides whether medicine or examination is needed.

Most often it is separation of the abdominal muscles, which is not a hole in the wall and does not become trapped, and much of it improves with time and physiotherapy. An umbilical hernia can occur alongside it, though, so an examination is needed to be sure. [7, 10]

Yes. An incisional hernia can appear at the scar months or years after the operation, and the chance is higher after wound infection and with excess weight and smoking. [8, 10]

No. A binder may feel comfortable, but it does not close the hole or treat the hernia, and it does not replace an examination to find out what type it is. [2, 4]

An assessment first is best. With muscle separation, a physiotherapist sets graded exercises that suit you, and some traditional exercises are postponed at first because they increase pressure on the middle of the abdomen. [7]

If the bulge becomes firm and painful and will not go back, or there is sudden severe pain, vomiting, inability to pass wind, or redness over the bulge. [2, 4, 5]

No. Nausea has many causes, and the clinician connects it with other symptoms, examination and tests before deciding whether the gallbladder is involved.

No. Findings are read with pain, complications, tests and health status, with coordination of pregnancy care when relevant.

Do not stop or change any medicine on your own. Bring a complete medicine and supplement list so the team can give instructions suited to you.

Usually not. NICE advises that stones causing no symptoms, in a normal gallbladder and bile ducts, do not need treatment unless symptoms develop. Your clinician decides based on your situation. [1]

The NHS describes it as possibly severe and constant, in the middle of the tummy or under the right ribs, lasting over 30 minutes and up to several hours. Similar symptoms can have other causes, so assessment decides. [8, 1]

Seek urgent help if pain lasts over 30 minutes or is sudden and severe, spreads to the back with vomiting, comes with high temperature or shivering, or with yellow skin or eyes. [8, 2]

Ultrasound is important, but NICE pairs it with liver function tests, and MRCP may be needed if a duct is dilated or tests are abnormal. Results are read alongside the history and examination. [1, 5]

No. A stone alone is not enough; symptoms, complications and assessment results determine whether removal is appropriate. [1, 5]

Not necessarily. It can be an intentional safety decision when the details of the case make an open approach safer. [2, 3, 10]

No. Ultrasound is important, but the surgeon combines it with symptoms, examination, blood results, health history and sometimes additional tests. [1, 2]

Recovery after laparoscopic surgery is often quicker, with a shorter hospital stay, but this varies between people and with the reason for surgery and overall health. The team gives you the recovery plan that fits you. [4, 5, 8]

Bring the ultrasound report, dated blood tests, a list of medicines and supplements, and a note of when pain attacks happen and how long they last. If you have had abdominal operations before, bring their reports. [1, 2, 5]

After laparoscopic surgery, if the skin was closed with sutures, staples or glue, MedlinePlus says you may remove the dressings and shower the day after surgery; if tape strips were used, cover the wounds with plastic wrap when showering for the first week [3]. Do not soak in a bathtub or hot tub or go swimming until your surgeon says it is OK [3]. Open surgery or a drain comes with different instructions, so your team's written sheet is the reference [3, 8]. If the wound becomes red, drains, or you develop a fever, contact the team [3].

After laparoscopic surgery, wound pain eases gradually, and many people feel pain in one or both shoulders. This comes from the gas left in the belly after the operation and should ease over several days to a week [3]. Returning to desk work may be possible after about one to two weeks, depending on the job and the type of surgery [2, 3]. Pain not controlled by the prescribed medicine, pain that worsens rather than eases, or pain with fever, yellowing or persistent vomiting is not ordinary recovery, so contact the team [2, 3].

Follow the progression and team instructions, because food return depends on the procedure, tolerance and health situation. Do not rely on a general online list. [2, 3, 7]

Bowel change can have several causes after surgery. If it persists or is severe, or comes with dehydration, pain or fever, contact the team for assessment in your context. [2, 3, 4]

Do not increase or change medicine on your own. Increasing pain may require a question about the cause, and the team decides whether medicine or examination is needed. [2, 7, 10]

There is no single date for everyone. The answer depends on the type of operation, pain, medicines that cause drowsiness and the surgeon's instructions. Ask the team before returning to driving or lifting, and describe the nature of your work. [2, 3, 8]

Yellowing after surgery needs urgent assessment, especially with fever or abdominal pain, because it can be related to the bile ducts. Do not wait for the routine follow-up; seek urgent care and bring the operation report. [2, 9, 10]

Usually severe pain in the upper right or middle abdomen, often after eating, lasting up to several hours, with nausea or vomiting. Fever, yellowing of the eyes or skin, or constant pain need same-day assessment, and upper abdominal pain in pregnancy also needs a blood pressure check so preeclampsia is not missed. [3, 4, 9]

No. Nausea has many causes and is interpreted with pain pattern, examination and results rather than the gallbladder alone. Seek earlier assessment if it comes with severe pain, repeated vomiting or warning signs. [3, 4]

No. Ultrasound is important for gallbladder assessment, but the decision combines symptoms, complications, tests, examination and pregnancy stage with care-team coordination. [1, 6, 8]

Do not change or stop a medicine on your own. Bring a complete medicine and supplement list, and follow the clinician's or maternity team's instructions for any change. [5, 8]

Ultrasound uses sound waves rather than ionising radiation, which is why it is a first-line test for gallbladder assessment in pregnancy. That does not mean it should be done without a reason; the clinician requests it when there is a clear question to answer. [2, 5, 7]

When surgery is clearly needed, surgical society guidance such as SAGES states that laparoscopic gallbladder removal can be performed during pregnancy with specific precautions. Timing and approach are still decided jointly by the surgeon and the maternity team according to the case and pregnancy stage, not by a general rule. [6, 8, 10]

Fully formed gallstones do not typically disappear on their own [1, 2]. Medical dissolution therapies, such as oral bile acid medications, have very limited clinical effectiveness and are only considered in narrow circumstances for specific small, non-calcified stones in individuals who cannot undergo surgery [4, 5]. Because stones frequently recur after non-surgical treatment is stopped and the process requires long treatment periods, medication is not a routine substitute for surgery [4, 5].

Current clinical guidelines do not recommend repetitive serial ultrasound surveillance every six or twelve months solely to monitor documented silent gallstones [1, 6]. In the absence of new symptoms, frequent routine scanning rarely alters management and tends to cause unnecessary health anxiety [1]. The recognized evidence-based approach is expectant management: living normally without anxiety or dietary deprivation, while remaining clearly informed about genuine biliary symptoms so you know when a medical assessment is needed [1, 2, 3].

Uncomplicated biliary colic is a transient mechanical pain episode caused by temporary ductal impaction; it typically resolves within one to several hours without causing persistent wall inflammation or fever [2, 10]. In contrast, acute cholecystitis occurs when prolonged ductal obstruction leads to sustained intraluminal hypertension, mucosal ischemia, and bacterial inflammation, resulting in continuous severe pain lasting several hours, fever, elevated white blood cell counts, and prominent inflammatory changes visible on ultrasound [1, 6, 10].

No, gallbladder removal does not usually require permanent elimination of dietary fats [5, 8]. The liver continues producing bile continuously, discharging it directly into the small intestine, and digestive habits generally return to normal over time [5, 7]. During early recovery, moderating very rich or fried foods and eating smaller, balanced meals can help minimize temporary digestive looseness while your body adapts [5, 8, 11].

No. A silent stone without symptoms, with a normal gallbladder and ducts and no added risk features, usually needs follow-up rather than preventive surgery. [1, 3, 4]

Yes, specific groups such as a single large stone, a fully calcified gallbladder, a large or growing polyp, haemolytic disease, or immunosuppression/organ transplantation may prompt a discussion of earlier surgery based on your situation. [4, 5, 10]

No. Size is one factor among several, alongside age, symptoms, complications and your overall health. There is no safe rule based on size alone. [4, 5]

Uncommon, but possible. Severe pain, fever, jaundice, repeated vomiting or dark urine need prompt assessment according to severity rather than waiting. [1, 2, 6]

Bile acid medicines can break up small cholesterol stones, but this may take months or years and stones can come back even after treatment. A stone that causes no symptoms usually needs no treatment at all, so do not start a medicine yourself; ask the clinician whether it has any place in your case. [7]

No, that is a different question. Reassurance that a silent stone needs no treatment applies to stones in a normal gallbladder and normal bile ducts. For stones in the common bile duct, NICE recommends bile duct clearance and laparoscopic gallbladder removal even without symptoms, so the decision is made with the surgeon. [1]

Usually around an hour to an hour and a half, but the time in hospital is longer because of preparation and recovery. Severe inflammation can make the operation longer. [4, 8]

Many people go home the same day after keyhole surgery, and some stay one night. It depends on your condition, the hospital, and having someone to take you home and stay with you for the first 24 hours. [4, 5]

Do not stop any medicine on your own. The team decides at the pre-operative assessment what should be stopped or adjusted and when, and gives you written instructions. [5, 9]

Yes, it is common after keyhole surgery because of the gas used to inflate the abdomen, and it usually eases within a day or two. Severe or worsening abdominal pain, however, needs contact with the team. [6, 8]

Usually, yes. The liver keeps making bile, and some people notice discomfort with fatty food or diarrhoea at first, which usually improves with time. [4, 6]

Yes, especially a small groin hernia in women or a Spigelian hernia on the side of the abdomen. Sometimes the only symptom is pain at a specific spot, and ultrasound can help when the examination is unclear. [6, 10]

Usually not. Many hernias are painless, or cause heaviness and dragging that builds at the end of the day and with effort and eases with rest. Sudden, severe, constant pain is different and needs emergency care. [2, 5, 9]

Muscle separation causes a long ridge down the middle of the abdomen with no hole in the wall, and it shows when you tense your abdominal muscles. A hernia is a bulge at a specific point that may grow when you cough. Telling them apart for certain needs an examination. [7, 10]

Not always. Most hernias are diagnosed by examination while you stand and cough. Ultrasound or CT is used when the examination is unclear, or before planning the repair of an incisional or large hernia. [1, 6, 8]

The first step is an examination to find out what type it is. Some inguinal hernias in men with few symptoms can be watched, while a femoral hernia, or a groin hernia in a woman, is usually recommended for repair. [2, 6]

Frequently asked questions

Bariatric Surgery

Generally when BMI is 40 or above, or 35 or above with an associated condition such as diabetes or sleep apnoea, and after other routes to weight loss have been tried without success. The assessment at the clinic is what establishes this precisely for your case.

A sleeve is a permanent surgical procedure that changes the size of the stomach. The injections are a medication that can be stopped when we decide to stop it. The injections have become a genuine alternative for many cases that would once have gone to surgery: but not for every case, and that is exactly what the assessment establishes.

Yes, if habits do not change. Surgery creates an opportunity, but what holds the result is the correct dietary progression, follow-up and long-term commitment. That is why post-operative nutrition follow-up is a core part of the plan, not an add-on.

As with any surgical procedure, yes: the main ones being vitamin and mineral deficiency, reflux, and the general risks of surgery. But in the cases that warrant surgery, the risks of the obesity itself are greater. The surgeon explains the risks specific to your case in detail before any decision.

It may suit selected cases, but first review the procedure, weight course, food, symptoms, nutrient status and medicines. The surgical and weight-management teams establish whether the cause is behavioural, medical or procedure-related and whether medicine or another step is appropriate.

Yes. Tell the team because it may indicate sleep apnoea and affect anaesthetic assessment and follow-up. Do not wait for surgery to investigate it; a sleep study and treatment may be needed beforehand, depending on symptoms and results.

The plan depends on the procedure and surgeon's instructions. Texture and portions progress after surgery, with attention to protein, fluids and prescribed supplements. Do not copy another person's schedule, and contact the team promptly if you cannot drink, vomit repeatedly or have increasing pain.

Because follow-up reviews nutrition, blood tests, supplements, medicines and symptoms, not weight alone. [6, 8, 9]

Yes. Reduced intake and altered tolerance can cause deficiency even without intestinal bypass. [7, 8, 9]

Agree clear responsibility within shared care and keep the operation report and follow-up schedule. BOMSS recommends at least annual monitoring after the first two years. [8, 9]

Do not stop medicine yourself; the clinician reviews readings and symptoms and adjusts treatment safely. [1, 2]

Not necessarily. It calls for a respectful review of medical, nutritional, behavioural and anatomical factors without blame. [2, 4, 6]
