Bring the operation report, medicine and supplement lists, recent results and a clear symptom description. [2, 8, 9]

BOMSS guidance advises avoiding pregnancy for the first 12 to 18 months after surgery, and telling the team early about any plan so tests and supplements can be reviewed. [8, 9]

No. The removed portion of the stomach cannot be restored, which is why informed consent and discussion of alternatives matter before deciding. [5, 10, 12]

Not necessarily. Selection needs medical, nutritional and psychological assessment and an individual discussion of benefits, risks and alternatives. [1, 2, 4]

Not always. Reflux may persist or develop after a sleeve, so reflux before surgery matters when choosing a procedure and planning follow-up. [2, 12]

They are usually part of the plan, but type, dose and monitoring should be set by the team according to the procedure, intake and blood results. [7, 8, 9]

Chest pain, breathlessness, fever, a persistently fast pulse, increasing severe pain, repeated vomiting or inability to drink need urgent assessment. [3, 10, 12]

No. Food, supplements, blood tests, psychological health, activity and symptom review are parts of long-term care. [2, 6, 8, 9]

MedlinePlus states the operation takes 60 to 90 minutes and most people go home after about 2 days; the team decides based on your recovery. [10]

Cleveland Clinic reports an average of about 25% to 30% of body weight in the first 1 to 2 years, but this is an average, not a promise, and depends on habits after surgery. [12]

Do not change the plan independently; a result is read with the operation, plan and earlier results, and it may be normal precisely because the supplement is working. [1, 2]

Many post-operative plans include long-term supplementation and monitoring, but the type and details are set by the care team. [1, 2, 6]

BOMSS lists a full blood count, calcium, liver and kidney tests, B12 and folate, ferritin and vitamin D, with zinc, copper and selenium for sleeve and bypass. Your team may add or adjust tests for your situation. [2]

Yes, contact the team promptly rather than waiting. Persistent vomiting raises the risk of thiamine deficiency, which can develop within days and affect the nerves. [2, 3]

Yes. Guidance advises avoiding pregnancy until around 12 to 18 months after surgery, and a pregnancy needs prompt referral for consultant-led obstetric care. Vitamin A in the retinol form is avoided while the beta-carotene form is acceptable, and higher-dose folic acid starts before conception. Do not change supplements yourself; tell the team early. [2]

Anaemia symptoms can come from low iron, B12, folate or copper; hair loss from low zinc, iron or protein; numbness in the limbs or memory problems from low B12 or thiamine; and night blindness from low vitamin A. Do not self-treat with high doses; tests identify what is actually low. [2]

No. Texture progression and portions should follow your team, tolerance and symptoms. [10, 13]

Repeated vomiting or vomiting that prevents fluids needs prompt contact and assessment of the cause. [2, 8, 10]

No. Requirements and doses depend on procedure, intake, blood results and the clinical plan. [7, 8, 9]

Do not stop or change a dose by yourself; a result is interpreted with the plan and trend over time. [8, 9]

Difficulty keeping fluids down with marked dizziness, reduced urine or severe lethargy calls for prompt contact. [2, 10]

Nutritional and medical monitoring after bariatric surgery is long term and is adjusted to the procedure, results and symptoms. [6, 8, 9, 11]

BOMSS guidance recommends a B12 injection every 3 months after a sleeve even with a normal level to prevent deficiency; the final decision rests with your team. [8]

No. Tests are tailored to history, examination, conditions and the proposed procedure. [2, 3]

Do not stop a medicine yourself; the surgical and anaesthesia teams should give specific instructions. [2, 3]

It reviews expectations, support, eating patterns and factors affecting safety and follow-up; it is not there to judge you. [4]

No. When prescribed, its purpose, timing and medicine monitoring are tailored to your circumstances. [2, 3]

Follow the centre’s list and bring medicines, reports and equipment specifically requested by the team. [2, 3]

No. A delay may allow treatment of a problem, improved safety or a clearer plan. [2, 3, 4]

ERAS recommendations say at least 4 weeks before surgery, and earlier is better. Ask for help if it is difficult, because support and nicotine replacement make a difference. [3]

NIDDK lists a body mass index of 40 or more, 35 or more with a serious health problem, or 30 or more with hard-to-control type 2 diabetes; the final decision follows team assessment. [13]

No. It is one part of a picture that includes conditions, medicines, nutrition, sleep, psychological health, expectations and risk. [1, 2, 13]

Composition varies, but it commonly combines surgery, medicine, nutrition, psychological care and anaesthesia according to need. [2, 3, 4]

It identifies support needs and treatable risks; sometimes it recommends more preparation before a decision, which is not a judgement of the person. [4]

No. Testing follows history, examination, procedure and the questions that need answering. [2, 3, 9]

Choice should consider anatomy, conditions, reflux, risks, preferences and follow-up rather than the procedure name alone. [1, 2, 5]

Usually information, treatment or support remains incomplete; ask for the next step, responsible person and a review point. [2, 4]

No. Follow the written anaesthesia and surgical instructions because conditions and medicines can change the plan. [2, 3]

Usually, yes, but the surgeon should explain the plan and when safety could require a change. [5, 10, 12]

Yes. Gradual early movement lowers the risk of clots and chest problems, but its timing and limits are set by the team. [3, 10]

There is no single timetable for everyone; follow the written texture progression from the surgeon and dietitian. [10, 13]

Repeated vomiting or inability to keep fluids down needs prompt contact and assessment, not an unsupervised diet change. [10, 12]

Chest pain, breathlessness, fever, persistent fast pulse, increasing severe pain, bleeding and inability to drink require urgent assessment. [3, 10, 12]

Frequently asked questions

Dermatology & Aesthetics

Because the commonest causes of hair loss we see are iron and ferritin deficiency, vitamin D deficiency and thyroid dysfunction, none of which is solved by a topical product. Once we know the cause, treatment is faster, cheaper and more durable.

A direct one. Insulin resistance and PCOS show on the skin as hormonal acne and excess hair. Deficiencies in zinc, vitamin D and omega-3 show as dryness and shedding. That is why the dermatology and nutrition departments work together here.

They improve, but the expectation has to be realistic: recent marks (red) respond far better than old ones (white). The best approach is prevention: moisturising and tightening sessions while the weight is coming off, rather than afterwards.

Do not stop it yourself. Shedding may relate to the pace of loss, too little protein or energy, iron or thyroid problems, a scalp condition, or the medicine. Review timing, food and treatment with the prescriber, and arrange dermatology assessment for patches, inflammation or marked loss.

No. Hair loss is a symptom with different causes, and a local procedure does not automatically treat iron deficiency, thyroid disease or a scalp disorder. Diagnosis comes first; then the clinician can explain whether mesotherapy has a role, the limits of evidence, risks and alternatives.

Dark circles and dullness have many causes, and results depend on the cause and injected substance; there is no universal protocol or guarantee. Dermatology assessment separates pigment, vessels, allergy, volume loss or an internal cause and explains whether injection or another option is more appropriate.

Usually not. History and scalp examination determine whether a blood count, iron measures, thyroid testing or another investigation will answer a real question. Some causes are identified by pattern, and dermoscopy or scalp biopsy may matter more than broad blood testing [1, 5].

No. Inherited loss, alopecia areata, traction and several scalp diseases can occur with normal blood results. A normal result answers only the question that assay was designed to answer; pattern and examination remain essential [1, 2, 5].

Not always. Iron deficiency is considered according to symptoms, bleeding, intake and results, but it is one of many possibilities and can coexist with another pattern. Do not start iron on your own; excess can harm and the cause of deficiency should be understood [1, 13].

Do not apply one universal number. Timing depends on the product, amount, assay and laboratory method, and an urgent test may not be delayable. Give the clinician and laboratory all details, follow their instructions and do not stop prescribed treatment independently [8, 9, 14].

No. A shampoo may improve appearance or scale in selected situations, but it cannot diagnose the cause. A supplement may help a defined need, while excess nutrients can harm or confuse testing. Treatment follows identification of the pattern and cause [1, 3, 9].

No. Interference is linked to selected assays that use biotin-sensitive technology and varies by instrument, amount and timing. Do not assume every result is wrong or unaffected; disclose the supplement so the clinician and laboratory can review the method [1, 3, 5].

The warning here concerns laboratory measurement: biotin can make certain thyroid-function results look abnormal without reflecting the true level. The clinician compares the result with symptoms and the assay method before changing treatment [4, 6].

There is no single interval for every product and assay. Amount, last-dose timing, analyser and urgency all matter. Ask the clinician and laboratory and follow their instructions; do not stop prescribed treatment or delay an urgent test independently [3, 13].

Contact the clinician or laboratory with the product name, amount and time of the last dose. Do not automatically discard or repeat the result yourself; they review the assay and context and decide whether repetition at another time or by another method is needed [3, 7].

Not automatically. Biotin deficiency is rare, and evidence for hair benefit without deficiency is limited. Identify the pattern and examine the scalp first; then determine whether there is a deficiency or another cause needing different care [2, 9, 10].

Do not stop prescribed medicine on your own. Shedding may relate to the pace of loss, reduced intake, or an independent cause, and a direct drug effect is not established in every case. Ask the prescriber to review timing, benefits, risks, and any appropriate adjustment [1, 4].

Not necessarily. Telogen effluvium is often noticed after the trigger because the hair cycle changes before shedding becomes visible. Record illness, stress, and the pace of loss over preceding months rather than focusing on the latest day alone [2, 11].

Not without evidence of deficiency. The AAD advises iron, zinc, or biotin when testing confirms a low level, because excess can be harmful or interfere with care. History and examination determine which test is appropriate [3].

Shedding generally involves whole hairs released from the scalp, while breakage leaves hairs of different lengths. Home inspection is not always enough, especially with patches, scale, or pain; examination clarifies the distinction [7, 12].

If the cause is temporary telogen effluvium and the trigger resolves, hair often improves gradually, but there is no guaranteed timetable. Persistent shedding or a widening part may indicate another or additional cause and needs assessment [2, 5].

Bring medicines and supplements, start dates and changes, an approximate weight and food record, illness, fever, surgery or stress, and consistent scalp photographs. History and examination guide whether tests or referral are needed [7].

No. Acne develops within hair follicles through interactions involving sebum, shed skin cells, and inflammation; it is not caused by poor cleanliness. Regular gentle cleansing helps, while repeated washing and scrubbing can irritate skin and make breakouts look worse [1,5,7].

No. Mild dryness can occur with some treatments, but persistent burning, cracking, or swelling does not measure effectiveness. Review the method and routine with a clinician or pharmacist instead of increasing the amount or combining irritating ingredients [1,3,8].

It can, especially when a lesion is deep or the skin is prone to pigmentation. Squeezing adds injury and inflammation, increasing the chance of a post-inflammatory mark or scar. Leave it alone and seek assessment if it is painful or recurrent [1,2,9].

If acne is deep, painful, or scarring, or if there is no improvement after the agreed period of correct consistent use, assessment is better than adding random products. Effects on mood, school, or daily life are also valid reasons to seek help [4,5,8,11].

No. A flat colour change is usually a post-inflammatory mark and may fade, while a depression or raised area is a textural change more consistent with scarring. Assessment distinguishes them and avoids an aggressive procedure that is poorly timed or unsuitable for the skin [2,13,16,17].

No. A clinician selects tests when the history includes clues such as sudden onset in a woman or girl together with irregular periods, excess hair, or other symptoms. Lesion location alone does not establish a hormonal cause [5,6,14,15].

No. A widening part is common in female pattern hair loss, but diffuse shedding and other causes can look similar or coexist. Scalp examination and history make the distinction [2, 3].

Childbirth is a recognized trigger of temporary telogen effluvium, often noticed after a delay. Patches, pain, scale, or an unexpectedly persistent problem need examination rather than assuming childbirth is the only cause [4, 7].

Not routinely in every case. Irregular periods, increased facial hair, or acne may direct specific tests, while another pattern may need scalp examination, iron assessment, or thyroid testing. History and examination select the work-up [3, 7].

It is better not to guess. Supplementation should follow confirmed deficiency or a clear clinical reason, and biotin can interfere with some laboratory results. Tell the clinician and laboratory about every supplement before testing [3].

Yes. Repeated traction can cause traction alopecia, and some cases become permanent when it continues for too long. A painful style or one pulling the edges should be loosened, and persistent thinning needs examination [8].

A sudden patch, eyebrow or eyelash loss, pain or burning, scale or discharge, and shiny scar-like skin all justify faster assessment. A smooth patch may fit alopecia areata, but a photograph alone is insufficient for diagnosis [10, 11].

It is common, but not every recession has the same cause or pace. Hereditary loss is usually gradual at the temples and crown, while patches, inflammation, or rapid shedding need a different explanation. If change is distressing or progressing quickly, examination can identify the pattern rather than relying on guesswork [1, 6, 9].

No. Family history is useful, but the clinician also considers distribution, speed, scalp findings, and medical history. Hereditary loss and another cause can coexist, so the pattern and examination matter more than the name of a relative with similar loss [2, 6, 8].

Not necessarily. A clear hereditary pattern may be identified from history and examination. Tests are targeted when diffuse shedding, systemic symptoms, restricted intake, recent illness, or suspected deficiency or hormonal disorder makes them useful. A test should answer a clinical question rather than form a fixed panel for everyone [2, 8, 9].

Usually not. A smooth round patch may be alopecia areata, scale with broken hairs may raise concern for infection, and pain or scarring changes the priority. Diagnosis requires scalp examination and sometimes magnification or targeted testing [7, 10, 11].

It is better not to. A supplement can address a defined need but does not treat every pattern, and excessive amounts of some nutrients can cause harm or worsen loss. Tell the clinician and laboratory about biotin and other supplements before testing, and do not let marketing replace assessment of the cause [2, 3, 4].

No. Cutting changes shaft length, not the follicle cycle, and washing less does not stop the cause. Hairs already ready to shed may collect and appear together during washing. Gentle care reduces breakage and traction, but treatment of the cause depends on diagnosis [2, 4, 5].

No. Stress is a possible trigger, not a diagnostic test. The clinician reviews timing, distribution, scalp appearance, medicines, diet, and systemic symptoms. Pattern loss, alopecia areata, breakage, or inflammation can coincide with a stressful period, so examination matters [1, 3, 4, 5].

Follicles affected during illness enter a resting phase before the hair is released, so shedding is not immediate. This delay is part of the hair cycle, and recovery may precede the extra hair seen in the shower. It explains timing but does not replace assessment if the pattern is unusual [1, 2, 3].

The expected pattern is diffuse thinning, not one round bald patch. Patches, lost beard or eyebrow hair, heavy scale, or scarring need examination for other causes such as alopecia areata, infection, or inflammation. A photograph alone should not label a patch as telogen effluvium [1, 6, 7, 11].

No. Cutting changes shaft length but not the follicle cycle. Less frequent washing allows hairs already ready to shed to collect and appear together. Gentle washing and combing reduce breakage, but settling of true shedding depends on the trigger ending and any confirmed cause being addressed [1, 3, 10].

Not without assessment. Iron should address a demonstrated need with appropriate follow-up, while biotin does not treat every shedding pattern and can interfere with some tests. Random supplementation can obscure the real cause or cause harm, so disclose everything you take before investigations are chosen [2, 5, 6].

You may notice shedding gradually decrease, followed by short new hairs and slow improvement in density. Spaced photographs in consistent lighting are more useful than daily mirror checks. If shedding continues for many months, worsens, or is joined by pain, patches, or scarring, return for diagnostic reassessment [1, 2, 3].

No. Acne develops within hair follicles through interactions involving sebum, shed skin cells, and inflammation; it is not caused by poor cleanliness. Regular gentle cleansing helps, while repeated washing and scrubbing can irritate skin and make breakouts look worse [1,5,7].

No. Mild dryness can occur with some treatments, but persistent burning, cracking, or swelling does not measure effectiveness. Review the method and routine with a clinician or pharmacist instead of increasing the amount or combining irritating ingredients [1,3,8].

It can, especially when a lesion is deep or the skin is prone to pigmentation. Squeezing adds injury and inflammation, increasing the chance of a post-inflammatory mark or scar. Leave it alone and seek assessment if it is painful or recurrent [1,2,9].

If acne is deep, painful, or scarring, or if there is no improvement after the agreed period of correct consistent use, assessment is better than adding random products. Effects on mood, school, or daily life are also valid reasons to seek help [4,5,8,11].

No. A flat colour change is usually a post-inflammatory mark and may fade, while a depression or raised area is a textural change more consistent with scarring. Assessment distinguishes them and avoids an aggressive procedure that is poorly timed or unsuitable for the skin [2,13,16,17].

No. A clinician selects tests when the history includes clues such as sudden onset in a woman or girl together with irregular periods, excess hair, or other symptoms. Lesion location alone does not establish a hormonal cause [5,6,14,15].

No. Acne develops within hair follicles through interactions involving sebum, shed skin cells, and inflammation; it is not caused by poor cleanliness. Regular gentle cleansing helps, while repeated washing and scrubbing can irritate skin and make breakouts look worse [1,5,7].

Usually, strong ongoing itching is not a typical feature of acne. Inflamed acne can feel tender or sore, but itching is rarely the main complaint [1, 8, 11]. Similar-looking small bumps that itch, especially on the upper chest, back, shoulders, or hairline, may make a clinician consider folliculitis, including Malassezia folliculitis, or contact irritation. An examination is still needed because symptoms can overlap [2, 3, 8].

Acne antibiotics act against bacteria, not yeast or fungi [2, 4, 8]. Broad-spectrum antibiotics can change the normal balance of organisms on the skin. With less bacterial competition, Malassezia yeast may grow more easily inside follicles and an itchy outbreak can become worse [2, 4, 8].

Shaving bumps, or pseudofolliculitis barbae, happen when a closely cut curved hair grows back into nearby skin. The bumps therefore follow the place and timing of close shaving [5, 6]. Bacterial folliculitis is an infection within a follicle and may cause tender pus-filled spots, including on skin that has not been shaved. A clinician can assess the pattern and decide whether an antiseptic or another treatment is appropriate [7, 9].

No. Rough scrubbing or popping can break the follicle wall and push inflammation, pus, and germs deeper into the skin, which may increase the risk of painful abscesses [1, 9, 10]. This trauma can also leave dark marks after the bump settles. Gentle washing with a mild cleanser and your hands is a safer approach [1, 5, 9, 10].

Book a dermatology assessment if the bumps last more than two weeks despite gentle care, if itching interrupts sleep or daily life, if they flare after acne antibiotics, or if they leave dark marks or scars [1, 2, 7, 8]. Fever, worsening pain, or spreading redness needs same-day urgent medical care. The clinician can examine the skin, review your history and medicines, decide whether further tests are needed, and give you a written plan [1, 7, 8, 12].

No. Acne develops within hair follicles through interactions involving sebum, shed skin cells, and inflammation; it is not caused by poor cleanliness. Regular gentle cleansing helps, while repeated washing and scrubbing can irritate skin and make breakouts look worse [1,5,7].

It can be: thick, velvety darkening in the neck folds (acanthosis nigricans) is often linked to insulin resistance and can be a sign of prediabetes. But insulin resistance usually has no symptoms, so the neck neither confirms nor rules it out; blood tests chosen by a clinician answer the question. [2, 6, 11]

No. Acanthosis nigricans can be linked with insulin resistance or diabetes in some people, but it proves neither and needs to be read alongside age, symptoms and appropriate tests. [1, 3, 10]

No. It is not dirt, and harsh rubbing or strong products can irritate the skin and darken it further. Start with assessment of the cause and gentle care, and ask a qualified clinician before any medicated cream. [1, 4, 5]

There is no single test that suits everyone; clinicians choose tests such as glucose tests according to age, symptoms, risk factors and medicines. [6, 9]

If the darkening appears suddenly or spreads quickly, or comes with unexplained weight loss, pain, a sore or clear general illness, or if it affects a child or occurs in pregnancy. [1, 2, 5]

No. Colour change alone does not diagnose gestational diabetes. Diagnosis relies on blood tests selected by the pregnancy-care team; mention the appearance, symptoms and risk factors at follow-up, and keep the testing appointment your team has set. [6, 7]

Pregnancy hormones increase pigment, and the neck is one of the areas that can darken; many people simply notice it later in pregnancy. Darker lines in the natural neck creases with smooth skin usually fit pigment and friction, while thick, velvety skin in the folds should be mentioned at follow-up. [2, 3, 12]

No. Scrubbing and irritating substances can inflame skin and worsen pigmentation. Use gentle care, and seek clinical advice before any medicated or lightening cream in pregnancy. [3, 9, 10]

Some pigmentation can fade with time after birth, but improvement varies and there is no guaranteed timetable. If the change persists or skin is thick or bothersome, raise it at postpartum follow-up or with a dermatologist. [1, 2]

Tell the team the same day about severe itch, especially on the palms or soles or when it disrupts sleep. Seek faster care for a painful rash, facial swelling or breathing difficulty. [1, 11]

Pregnancy acne often settles gradually in the months after birth as hormone levels change again [1, 2, 8]. It can continue for some people during the postpartum period because hormones, breastfeeding, sleep, and stress are still changing. A dermatologist can then review options that fit with breastfeeding rather than assuming every treatment is suitable [1, 3, 4].

Stop the product and contact the obstetrician and the clinician who prescribed it. Absorption from topical retinol or a topical retinoid is usually low, and limited accidental exposure does not mean that harm has occurred, but the product and timing still need a proper review [1, 3, 4]. Share the name, strength, amount, and dates used so the team can document the exposure and advise on pregnancy follow-up and alternatives [1, 2, 3].

Topical azelaic acid is often considered during pregnancy because skin absorption is low and available safety information is reassuring. It can help reduce acne inflammation and may improve dark marks or melasma [1, 2, 3, 4]. A clinician should still confirm the strength, product, and rest of the routine, especially if the skin is irritated or other active ingredients are being used [1, 2, 3].

Mild local itching can happen around inflamed spots or stretched skin [1, 11, 12]. Cholestasis is more likely to cause intense itching on the palms and soles, often worse at night and without a visible rash at first. This pattern needs same-day contact with the maternity team for liver-function and bile-acid blood tests; some people may need hospital assessment [11].

Many clinicians advise postponing strong chemical peels and cosmetic laser treatment until after birth because pregnancy can make pigment changes and irritation harder to predict [1, 2, 7]. Care during pregnancy usually focuses on gentle skincare and medicines with better pregnancy safety information. Any procedure should be discussed with the dermatologist and obstetrician rather than booked as routine acne care [1, 2, 4].

Melasma is a long-term condition that can return after the color fades. Treatment may lighten the patches to different degrees, but the skin can make pigment again after sun exposure or some hormonal changes [1, 2, 8]. Daily sun protection, including a suitable tinted sunscreen, and a maintenance plan may help preserve improvement and reduce relapse [2, 3, 11].

A clear broad-spectrum sunscreen protects against UVA and UVB, but it usually does not protect against visible light to the same degree [3, 4, 5]. A tinted sunscreen with iron oxides absorbs or scatters some visible light, mainly from the sun, so it may be more helpful for some people with melasma [2, 3, 4, 11].

No. Hydroquinone is a treatment rather than an everyday cosmetic moisturizer. Using it for months without follow-up can cause irritation or worsening color and can increase the risk of exogenous ochronosis, a blue-gray discoloration that is hard to treat [2, 6, 10]. A doctor should set the strength, course length, and whether a treatment break is needed [2, 6, 9].

Melasma manifests as symmetrical, reticulated brownish patches across the forehead, cheeks, and upper lip, closely associated with ultraviolet exposure and hormonal shifts without antecedent tissue damage [2, 11, 12]. In contrast, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation occurs strictly at the anatomical sites of prior cutaneous injury, such as resolved acne papules, burns, or harsh chemical peeling, lacking symmetric distribution [1, 8, 12].

Seek urgent assessment if a pigmented spot is asymmetrical, has irregular notched borders or several colors, grows quickly, bleeds, develops an ulcer, or causes persistent itching [11, 12]. These signs need prompt examination; the doctor then decides whether a biopsy is needed to rule out melanoma [2, 11, 12].

No. Eczema itself is not an infection and does not spread by touch, shared bedding, or spending time with someone who has it [8, 9, 10]. It is an inflammatory condition involving the skin barrier and immune system and may run in families, so several relatives can have eczema without passing it between them [1, 3, 8].

Apply a thin layer only to the inflamed areas, using the strength and duration the doctor prescribed. Many courses last about one to two weeks, but the plan varies by body site, age, and flare severity [1, 4, 8, 11]. Short use as directed usually has a low risk of side effects, while excessive or prolonged use can thin the skin, so check with the doctor if the flare does not settle [1, 4, 5].

Seek same-day urgent medical care if painful, dented blisters spread quickly, especially on the face, with fever or feeling unwell; this may be eczema herpeticum [6, 7, 9]. Do the same for widespread pus or honey-colored crusts, or redness and peeling over most of the body with chills. Some people with these signs need hospital admission and treatment by mouth or through a vein [6, 7, 9].

No. Broad food restriction is not recommended. Eczema involves the skin barrier and inflammation, and an unguided elimination diet may not improve the skin and may expose a child to nutritional deficiency or slower growth [8, 9, 11]. A doctor may arrange an allergy assessment when clear, rapid symptoms repeatedly follow a particular food and can advise whether testing or avoidance is appropriate [8, 11].

A thin lotion contains more water, so it spreads easily but may evaporate faster, and some ingredients can sting cracked skin [1, 4, 10]. A petrolatum-based ointment or ceramide-rich cream contains more oil and often holds moisture longer. The best choice is a fragrance-free product that the skin tolerates and that can be used regularly [1, 4, 8, 10].
